articles.title: Just-in-Time Neuromodulation: A Precision, State-Dependent Paradigm for On-Demand Brain Intervention
articles.authors: Ashkan Rashedi; Aref Pariz; Jing Jin; Marzieh Zare; ANDRE RUSSOWSKY BRUNONI; Hamed Ekhtiari
articles.abstract: Neuromodulation is commonly delivered on fixed schedules, whereas psychiatric and neurological symptoms fluctuate over time. Just-in-Time Neuromodulation (JiT-NM) offers a framework for aligning intervention with the emergence or escalation of clinically relevant neural or symptomatic states. We propose three essential components: targeting the desired state, a state-detection system, and a neuromodulatory intervention capable of acting within a clinically useful time window. A fourth, optional component, adaptive personalization, may refine detection models and stimulation parameters over time. JiT-NM may support self-initiated or autonomous delivery, open-loop or closed-loop control, informed by automated symptom recognition or self-report, physiological signals, digital phenotyping, or wearable neural sensing. Established responsive and adaptive implanted stimulation systems provide clinical precedents, while early investigations in psychiatric disorders support further exploration. We discuss how neuroimaging-derived targets and biomarkers might be translated into compact, individualized sensing-and-stimulation systems, emphasizing the need to validate reliable state detection with fewer sensors. Key challenges include demonstrating the added value of intervention timing, accommodating changing neural dynamics, establishing real-world usability, as well as addressing safety, privacy, and regulatory requirements. JiT-NM provides a framework for investigating whether on-demand, state-based stimulation can complement scheduled treatment or achieve superior outcomes while reducing unnecessary treatment burden.

articles.title: How Does Profile Text Signal Desirability in Online Dating? A Meta-Analysis of Cue Valence and Explicitness
articles.authors: Junwen M. Hu
articles.abstract: Signaling mate desirability is central to a well-functioning online dating market. This meta-analysis examines how profile text signals the owner's desirability. Drawing on research on negativity and cue diagnosticity, warranting theory, and signaling theory, I test how the valence (positive vs. negative) and explicitness (explicit vs. implicit) of text-based cues shape viewers' reactions. I analyzed 13 experiments (53 effect sizes) drawn from a scoping review of online dating research. Text-based cues have a small, heterogeneous effect on evaluations, dating intentions, and behavior toward the profile owner (g = 0.25). Negative cues move responses (g = 0.38), whereas positive cues do not (g = −0.07). Explicit and implicit cues do not differ overall, but the gap between negative and positive cues is larger for explicit cues. The results show that strategic verbal content in online dating profiles works as a screening device, carrying meaningful information about undesirable traits in a partner.

articles.title: Changing moral beliefs and behaviors using human-AI dialogues
articles.authors: Joshua Paul White; Carter Allen; Lucius Caviola; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Moral beliefs are widely considered resistant to change, yet the rise of conversational AI offers new tools for moral persuasion. We report a preregistered experiment (N = 500) in which participants were randomly assigned to a 5-round conversation with an AI agent prompted to persuade them that either eating meat, or not giving to charity, is morally wrong. Conversations produced large and immediate shifts in moral beliefs in the intended direction (Cohen’s d = 0.37–0.48), along with corresponding behavioral effects: participants in the charity conversation condition donated 16.35% more of their bonus money to charity than participants in the meat conversation condition, while those in the meat conversation condition were 25.04 percentage points more likely to choose a plant-based over a beef burger voucher compared to those in the charity conversation condition. One month later, the effect on burger voucher choice remained significant, while other effects did not. NLP analysis of participant moral justifications and AI persuasive strategies suggests that moral persuasion was partly driven by factual correction—particularly in the meat domain, where factual appeals to the naturalness and biological necessity of meat eating were the most common among participants—alongside direct moral argumentation. These results demonstrate that human-AI dialogues can produce meaningful change in moral beliefs and behavior, raising important questions about the capacity of conversational AI to shape human values at scale.

articles.title: “Treat us as capable”: Neurodivergent youths’ perceptions on adult support in digital participation
articles.authors: Yvette Edelaar-Peeters; Rogier de Groot; I. Chaplinska; Sophie Mary; H.M. Koning Ina; Peter Nikken; Carlo Schuengel; Hendrien Lourine Kaal
articles.abstract: Digital participation is essential for neurodivergent youth. However, parents, teachers, and professionals often struggle to provide appropriate digital support. Like offline contexts, supporting neurodivergent youths’ online behaviors requires finding a balance between protection from potential risks and the promotion of autonomy and empowerment. Until now, scholars have predominantly focused on caregivers' perspectives. Therefore, in this study perceptions of these youngsters themselves are investigated. Survey data of 58 neurodivergent youth on experienced digital support were analyzed. Responses supported the distinction between enabling-authoritative support and restrictive-authoritarian support. Neurodivergent youth reported that parents and teachers more often applied enabling-authoritative support and indicated that they found this approach more effective. These findings underscore the importance of enabling rather than restrictive digital support also for neurodivergent youth, as digitalization opens up new opportunities for redressing their inequities in participation.

articles.title: Relational Calibration: A Framework for Dynamic Instructional Regulation in Complex Learning Environments
articles.authors: Delwin B. Carter
articles.abstract: Relational Calibration (RC) is a theoretical framework for organizing enacted instructor responses during ongoing instruction. It specifies three response dimensions: relational positioning, instructional posture, and real-time modulation. Interpersonal attunement coordinates these dimensions by linking emerging instructional evidence and its interpretation to enacted responses. The framework’s functional target is sustaining engagement with demanding intellectual work while preserving intellectual demand. Grounded in research on professional noticing, adaptive and responsive teaching, contingent scaffolding, interpersonal teacher behavior, relational competence, and instructional communication, RC brings relational, instructional, and expressive aspects of response into a common event-level representation. It distinguishes observable evidence, interpretation, enacted response, instructional architecture, the functional target, proposed mechanisms, subsequent outcomes, and measurement. These distinctions provide a basis for examining how instructors coordinate responses within particular instructional events and how those responses relate to engagement and preserved demand. The manuscript develops the framework’s theoretical foundations, dimensions, and coordinating process, then specifies a measurement and research agenda addressing event boundaries, response coding, independent criterion measurement, comparison with established frameworks, and enactment across instructional contexts.

articles.title: Neurodivergent Youth Online: Professional Needs, Capacities, and Challenges
articles.authors: Yvette Edelaar-Peeters; Rogier de Groot; I. Chaplinska; Sophie Mary; H.M. Koning Ina; Peter Nikken; Carlo Schuengel; Hendrien Lourine Kaal
articles.abstract: Healthcare professionals and educators have expressed a need for greater support in guiding neurodivergent youth in their digital lives. Professionals’ perceptions of the digital needs, opportunities, and risks of neurodivergent youth, and how these perceptions are translated into their own needs for support, using a mixed-methods design consisting of online questionnaires and focus group interviews was studied.  Key support needs included collaboration with parents, navigating professional responsibilities, and addressing the gap between digital knowledge and online behaviour.

articles.title: Replication Research
articles.authors: Kevin McManus
articles.abstract: Replication studies are essential for building cumulative knowledge in second language acquisition (SLA) research because they allow researchers to revisit, contextualize, and extend the findings of earlier studies. Rather than arguing for the value of replication, this chapter focuses on the replication research process itself. It begins with two core issues: deciding what study to replicate and what kind of replication to conduct (conceptual, approximate, close, or exact). It then considers the place of replication in qualitative research. The chapter reviews methodological considerations for planning a replication, supported by a set of planning questions, and for disseminating it through presentations and journal articles, including reporting standards. It then describes the practical relevance of replication for building confidence in findings before they are applied and for testing lab-based results in classrooms. The chapter closes with future directions: integrating replication into research programs, extending it beyond quantitative methods, improving planning and reporting, and adopting open research practices.

articles.title: The plurality of metacognition: Historical origins and research traditions
articles.authors: Mauricio Sebastián Barrientos
articles.abstract: Metacognition is commonly defined as the monitoring and control of one’s own cognition, yet the term covers related phenomena that differ in their theoretical organisation, assessment, and application. This historically oriented narrative review examines how the convergence of cognitive, developmental, and educational research traditions produced this plurality. It reconstructs the construct’s empirical and theoretical antecedents in memory monitoring, children’s knowledge of cognition, and strategic regulation of learning, and compares influential accounts in terms of their explanatory aims, central components, and levels of analysis. The comparison shows that different traditions came to emphasise metacognitive knowledge, experiences, monitoring, regulatory activity, or the functional relation between object- and meta-level cognition. These differences are interpreted not as competing definitions of an identical phenomenon, but as reflecting the distinct problems and methods from which each account developed. The review argues that metacognition is best approached as a historically assembled family of related but partially non-interchangeable facets, without assuming either complete unity or fragmentation. This interpretation clarifies why indicators derived from different traditions often diverge, and why specifying the facet, function, and level of analysis intended by the term should be a condition for cumulative research across theory, measurement, and application.

articles.title: Peer Transmission of Mental Health Information Increases ADHD Self-Diagnosis
articles.authors: Tanay Katiyar; George Gillett; Adam Hunt; Amanda M Ferguson; Alessia Pascale; Alberto Acerbi; Nikhil Chaudhary; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Increased sharing of mental health information online has intensified public concern that social media may amplify mental health self-diagnosis rates. While much work has examined the types of mental health information available online, little attention is paid to the mechanisms governing how this information is created and consumed. Taking a cultural evolutionary perspective, we posit that social media facilitates peer-to-peer transmission of psychiatric information in novel formats and provides new motivations to transmit such information; this alters the information people see and their reactions to it. We investigate this through an adapted transmission chain paradigm where participants sequentially modify and transmit Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) explanations amongst each other, allowing us to examine how self-diagnostic tendencies evolve during this process. Across four studies, we find that such transmission increases participants’ tendency to diagnose themselves, and another individual with subclinical traits, with ADHD. Participants’ tendency to recommend this other individual to seek professional help also increases. Transmission format (i.e. generating an example list versus narrative summary) and motivation (i.e. making an explanation for maximising likes versus accuracy) moderate some effects. These results indicate that peer-to-peer transmission may play a key role in determining psychiatric diagnostic trends and shaping the public understanding of mental health.

articles.title: Root Causes and Prevention of Mobility Device Damage During Air Travel: A Rapid Review
articles.authors: Zeyad Ghulam; Alison Whiting; Tilak Dutta
articles.abstract:
Objective: The primary objective of this rapid review is to identify peer-reviewed academic literature that discusses the root causes of mobility device damage and loss during air travel, and to synthesize the operational strategies for preventing this damage.
Introduction: Air travel provides essential access to education, healthcare, employment, and leisure. However, persons with disabilities remain vastly underrepresented among air travelers and overrepresented in aviation complaint statistics. A failure point in the accessible travel chain is the damage, loss, or delayed return of mobility devices. While general accessibility reviews categorize device damage as a physical barrier, few investigate the specific cargo-handling mechanisms, securement failures, and design limitations that cause these incidents.

Inclusion Criteria: This review will include peer-reviewed literature focusing on travelers who use mobility devices. The primary concept is the damage, loss, or delayed return of these devices, alongside proposed preventive strategies or root-cause analyses. The context is restricted to commercial air travel operations, including ground handling, cargo stowage, and terminal transfers.

Methods: This protocol strictly adheres to the Cochrane Rapid Review Methods Group recommendations. Searches will be executed in Medline, Scopus and Web of Science (Core Collection). Title and abstract screening, full-text reviews and data extraction will be managed in Nested Knowledge. To expedite the process, a primary reviewer will conduct screening and data extraction, with a secondary reviewer independently piloting tools, screening all excluded records, and verifying data and risk-of-bias assessments. Evidence will be synthesized narratively, prioritizing high-quality study designs to inform operational mitigation.

articles.title: Planning for Solitude in Retirement: A Theory of Planned Behavior Perspective on Alone Time in Older Adulthood
articles.authors: Becky Yarwood; Delali Konu; Pearl Tshimbalanga; Pin-Jo Chiu; Grace Coume; Zitao Gao; Zige Huang; Mingyao Xiong; Thuy-vy Thi Nguyen
articles.abstract: Retirement marks a significant life transition, often accompanied by the loss of structured work routines, and subsequently, an increase in alone time. This study interviewed 8 pre-retirees and 15 retirees using semi-structured interviews. Guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior, we asked participants to reflect on their attitudes toward solitude, other people’s judgement toward their time alone, and their perceived control over managing solitude during retirement. Thematic analysis revealed themes related to general changes after retirement, including shifts in identity, the desire to balance social connection and alone time, as well as themes concerning factors that shape solitude experiences, such as personal autonomy and financial stability. While some participants embraced solitude as an opportunity for personal growth and well-being, others faced challenges such as boredom and isolation. Findings suggest that achieving a balance between alone time and social engagement is critical to fostering positive experiences of solitude in retirement.

articles.title: What Is a Wrong Answer Worth? The Out-of-Sample Value of the Chosen Option in Multiple-Choice Tests
articles.authors: Santiago Rivadeneira Quintero; Klint Kanopka; Mateus Mazzaferro; Benjamin Domingue
articles.abstract: Right/wrong scoring of multiple-choice items discards information about which wrong option was chosen. IRT models that use the choice date from 1972, but evidence on its value has come mostly in sample, one test at a time. We compared option-level and right/wrong models on predicting the option chosen in held-out responses (log-loss, in bits) across 116 Item Response Warehouse tables (110 Brazilian), 469 TIMSS and PIRLS tests and 121 Czech exam forms. In the warehouse, modeling the chosen option gained 15.4 millibits per response over the 2PL, 1.36 times the gain from estimating item discrimination. Of the option's gain, 84% came from which wrong option was chosen, where right/wrong models use only distractor popularity; the rest, on whether the answer was right, was about a fifth of discrimination's gain. The gain was positive in all 116 warehouse tables, in 119 of 121 Czech forms and, with priors on both models, in 463 of 469 TIMSS and PIRLS tests; relative to discrimination, it ranged from 0.8 (Czech exams) to 1.5 (ENEM). By our declared measure, the gain peaked in the lowest ability deciles in most tables; per wrong answer, the choice improved prediction over distractor popularity most in the top decile.

articles.title: The Bilingual Creative Metaphor Task: A Psychometric Assessment of Metaphor Production in English and Spanish
articles.authors: Reet Patel; Hannah Meghan Merseal; Paul V DiStefano; Janet van Hell; Roger Beaty; Benjamin Goecke
articles.abstract: Metaphors are frequently used during communication, offering insight into creativity and cognition through figurative language. In bilingual individuals, metaphor production is influenced by language proficiency and cultural context. However, there is no psychometrically validated test measuring metaphor production ability beyond English. This study develops a tool to assess bilingual metaphor production using simple prompts (e.g., “The small dog is...”) that require original metaphors (e.g., “a tiny tornado”). Using automatic item generation with GPT-4, we generated 100 metaphor prompts, evenly split between English and Spanish. A sample of 160 Spanish-English bilinguals on Prolific provided responses. To evaluate metaphor originality, 100 Spanish-English bilingual raters scored responses using a planned missing data design. We applied a graded response model (GRM) to compute factor scores for each item and person, yielding sufficient rater agreement and measurement precision across both languages (Factor Determinacy Index = .77, ranging from .58 to .87). To further develop the assessment tool, additional factor analysis identified the most effective items, forming a short test of 10 items per language. This research provides a foundation for developing reliable and valid assessments of bilingual metaphor production, advancing the understanding of creative language use in multilingual populations and supporting linguistic assessment applications.

articles.title: Workplace Relationships and Artificial Intelligence
articles.authors: Maxine Parker; Celine Huang; Sekoul Krastev
articles.abstract: Generative AI is now embedded in how coworkers, leaders, and organizations communicate, yet its effects on the relationships among them are still poorly understood. This review synthesizes recent research on how an individual’s AI use changes the way others perceive, judge, and behave toward them, and shows that these effects can be explained by established theories of human-human interaction, including attribution theory, computers-as-social-actors, the integrative model of organizational trust, social exchange theory, and resource-based theories. The evidence suggests that observers often read AI use as a sign of disposition rather than circumstance, judging AI users as less competent, motivated, warm, and authentic, and that disclosure does not repair the resulting loss of trust. These perceptions carry over into behavior: coworkers reciprocate less, share less knowledge, and show less prosocial behavior toward AI users, while AI-related job insecurity, loneliness, and work alienation further strain ties among colleagues. AI use also loosens moral standards and shifts how blame is assigned, making people more critical of others’ work but more lenient toward misconduct. These effects are conditional rather than uniformly negative. AI can reduce loneliness, improve coordination, and prompt employees to invest more in emotionally supportive ties, and relational buffers such as leader-member exchange, shared leadership, and supervisor support can offset its costs. The review concludes that AI’s costs to workplace relationships run mainly through indirect pathways, not through the technology itself. It outlines organizational implications, including clear norms for when and why AI is used and protection of socially valued tasks, and identifies priorities for future research: longitudinal designs, team- and network-level studies, intervention research, and more diverse samples.

articles.title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
articles.authors: Douglas Guilbeault; Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan
articles.abstract: Two foundational aspects of human cognition, abstractness and gender, are typically examined as separable. Here, we find they are systematically linked throughout the entire space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet —  and across numerous measurement techniques — more abstract concepts are more associated with men, an effect which replicates in languages around the world. This pattern not only holds across conceptual domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, this bias emerges in human and AI responses in free association tasks, indicating its internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. The male abstraction bias may underlie and unify a range of stereotypes, evidencing gender as a core organizing dimension in conceptual space.

articles.title: Generative AI Successfully Captures Visual Mental Imagery
articles.authors: Zaynab Rehman; Wilma Bainbridge
articles.abstract: When reading a passage, one often conjures up mental images of the scenes unfolding in the text. How similar are people in what they visualize, and can we leverage artificial intelligence to access these visualizations? Here, we used AI-generated imagery in two experiments to study the content of 251 participants’ mental imagery after reading nonfiction texts. In Experiment 1, 125 participants read and created mental images from blurbs of news articles, then compared their mental images against AI-generated images and the real-world images originally used in the articles. Participants converged on the content of their mental visualizations, reached a consensus on how well images matched their mental visualizations, and consistently agreed that AI-generated images were more concordant with their mental images than real-world ones. In Experiment 2, 126 new participants were shown a regenerated set of images to test if concordance with mental imagery can improve after using AI to update the images based on participant feedback in Experiment 1. Participants continued to demonstrate meaningful convergence, remained in agreement about which images best captured their mental visualization, and indicated higher concordance for AI-generated images over AI-updated real-world ones. However, participants demonstrated overall lower and more inconsistent patterns of convergence, agreement, and concordance, suggesting a single iteration is sufficient for capturing the normative mental imagery experience. These results demonstrate that generative artificial intelligence is a tractable way to examine the content of one’s mental images.

articles.title: Framing, Analysis, Interpretation and Two Supplemental Tests for Exploring Serial Mediation Theories with Cross-Sectional Data
articles.authors: Carl F Weems
articles.abstract: Nonexperimental cross sectional data are frequently used to evaluate mediation and serial mediation hypotheses despite well established limitations for such tests. Associational Variable Analysis (AVA) was introduced to address this problem by reframing mediational language in terms of conditional associations and incremental variance. This paper extends the framing, analysis options, and interpretation guidance in AVA to help researchers improve the analysis and interpretation of studies exploring serial mediation type theories with cross-sectional data. Two supplemental analyses are proposed to aid in the interpretation of such data. One symmetric conditional attenuation, measuring redundancy among the proposed set of variables. The second conditional centrality focused on the proposed mediating variables to examine if they account for a disproportionate share of the conditional dependence relative to the putative independent and dependent variables. Two empirical illustrations are used to demonstrate the framing, set of additional analyses needed to help frame alternative interpretations, and the utility of the two analytic summaries in terms of fostering both the completeness and accuracy of interpretation of such tests and foster incremental science. The first example draws on the data used in the initial AVA paper and the second evaluates a published serial mediation model linking family atmosphere to suicidal ideation through attachment and cognitive flexibility. Code and details for conducting the analyses are provided in supplemental materials. Findings illustrate how the suggested estimates help clarify redundancy, differentiation, and structural organization within multivariable theories thereby providing interpretive guidance for cross sectional analyses where serial mediation conclusions are not defensible.

articles.title: Examining Social Emotion Regulation in Spanish-English Bilinguals
articles.authors: Tiffany Cao; Razia S. Sahi; Chantal A. Valdivia-Moreno; Erik C Nook
articles.abstract: People frequently turn to others for help managing their emotions. This process of social emotion regulation often unfolds via language: For example, support providers can verbally offer new perspectives that shift another person’s emotions. Inspired by research showing that emotional reactivity is lower in a bilingual’s second language (L2) than their first language (L1), we tested whether social emotion regulation was more effective in Spanish (L1) or English (L2) for Spanish-English bilinguals. We pre-registered countervailing hypotheses, as regulation could either be more effective in L1 (due to increased familiarity and fluency), L2 (due to decreased emotional intensity), or no different across languages. In 2024, we recruited 250 U.S.-based Spanish-English bilingual women who reported learning Spanish before (78.4%) or concurrently with English (21.6%) and demonstrated high Spanish and English proficiency. Participants were presented with negative images before hearing audio recordings either describing the negative contents of the image or reinterpreting those contents to be less negative (i.e., social reappraisal) in either Spanish or English. Participants reported lower negative affect overall on English than Spanish trials, extending prior work demonstrating reduced emotional intensity in L2. Interestingly, social reappraisals lowered participants’ negative affect in both languages, with no difference across languages. Thus, Spanish-English bilinguals like those tested here may equally benefit from social reappraisal in both languages. Results advance basic research on language and emotion, guide translational applications for this population, and prompt future research (e.g., identifying moderators or examining other bilingual groups).

articles.title: Interact VR: Examining Social-Affective Responses to Social Exclusion in Adolescents with Conduct Disorder
articles.authors: Nicholas D. Thomson; Samuel James West; Jessica J. James; Sophie Lyngesen Kjærvik
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Social exclusion is associated with adverse social and emotional consequences and is particularly relevant for adolescents with conduct disorder (CD), who experience disproportionately high rates of peer rejection and interpersonal difficulties. Although Cyberball has been widely used to study social exclusion, less is known about how adolescents respond to varying levels of exclusion, and few studies have examined these experiences using immersive virtual reality (VR). The present study provides initial validation evidence for Interact VR; an immersive VR paradigm adapted from Cyberball that examines multidimensional social-affective functioning across varying levels of social exclusion.
Method: Adolescents with CD aged 13 – 17 years (Mage = 15.75, 66.5% male) completed three Interact VR conditions: inclusion, subtle exclusion, and severe exclusion. Following each condition, participants completed self-report measures of perceived social regard, belonging, competence, meaningful existence, affective valence, arousal, control, and discrete emotions.  
Linear mixed-effects models examined differences across conditions, and repeated binary outcomes were analyzed using logistic regression models. 
Results: Increasing social exclusion produced systematic and theoretically coherent changes across multiple domains of social-affective functioning. Participants reported lower perceived social regard, belonging, meaningful existence, increasingly negative affective valence, lower perceived control, and had a greater likelihood of reporting sadness, anger and disgust, and reduced happiness as exclusion increased. Most outcomes distinguished inclusion, subtle exclusion, and severe exclusion, demonstrating sensitivity to varying levels of social exclusion. Competence differentiated only severe exclusion from the other conditions, subjective arousal decreased as exclusion increased, and fear did not differ across conditions. 
Conclusions: These findings provide initial validation evidence for Interact VR as an ecologically valid paradigm for investigating multidimensional social-affective responses to social exclusion. More broadly, the findings demonstrate that adolescents with CD distinguish between subtle and severe social exclusion across multiple domains of social-affective functioning, providing a richer understanding of how they subjectively experience social exclusion and a promising platform for investigating the social-affective processes underlying CD.

articles.title: The Future of Social (Dis)Connection
articles.authors: Micaela Rodriguez; Scott W. Campbell; Amie Michelle Gordon
articles.abstract: Over the next decades, the nature of and possibilities for social connection will rapidly evolve with advances in artificial intelligence, mixed-reality technologies, and pervasive digital integration. Accordingly, psychological science must update how it conceptualizes and measures social connection. Here, we advance a three-part conceptual framework for understanding social (dis)connection in contemporary and future environments. First, we situate social experiences within a dynamic relational ecosystem—a system of interaction partners and channels, ambient social cues, and sociocultural contexts that together shape connection. Second, we conceptualize “alone” and “together” not as binary states but as a gradient shaped by level of physical copresence and communication (shades of aloneness and togetherness). Third, we conceptualize discrete social interactions as multidimensional, characterized by features such as interaction partner, relationship type, medium, temporality, engagement, and volition. Building on this framework, we propose five testable predictions about how social (dis)connection may evolve in the coming decades: the decoupling of objective and subjective connection, the erosion of “pure” solitude, the increasing effortfulness and value of in-person interaction, the fragmentation of shared reality, and the growing taken-for-grantedness of connection. We conclude by discussing methodological and applied implications of this framework.

articles.title: Psychosocial factors, masculine norms and suicide risk among men at a university in Ireland
articles.authors: Aisling McGrath; Shane O'Donnell; Noel Richardson
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Understanding suicide risk among men requires attention to psychosocial experiences alongside the gendered expectations shaping their lives. This study examined associations between demographic, behavioural and psychosocial factors, conformity to masculine norms and suicide risk among men attending an Irish university.
Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 512 male university students assessed suicide risk using the Suicide Behaviours Questionnaire–Revised (SBQ-R), alongside demographic characteristics, health behaviours, psychosocial measures and Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory (CMNI) subscales. Hierarchical binary logistic regression examined associations with scoring at or above the SBQ-R screening threshold (≥7), entering demographic and behavioural characteristics, psychosocial factors and masculine norms sequentially.
Results: Results: Of 473 participants with available SBQ-R data, 42.5% scored at or above the screening threshold; 64.5% of those with loneliness data met the loneliness criterion. Participants at or above the SBQ-R threshold reported greater emotional control, violence, playboy and self-reliance norms, lower endorsement of status and work-related norms, and less favourable help-seeking attitudes and intentions. In the fully adjusted model, higher loneliness (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.24, 95% CI 1.03–1.48) and hopelessness (aOR 1.23, 95% CI 1.04–1.45) were associated with higher odds of scoring at or above the threshold, while greater resilience was associated with lower odds (aOR 0.50, 95% CI 0.33–0.75). Heterosexual identification was associated with lower odds than non-heterosexual identification (aOR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21–0.93), while drug use was associated with higher odds than no use (aOR 2.00, 95% CI 1.08–3.71). Psychosocial factors significantly improved model fit (p < .001); masculine norm subscales did not (p = .780).
Discussion: The findings highlight relational experiences, future expectations and coping resources alongside inequalities among men as relevant to suicide prevention interventions in the university setting. The limited additional contribution of masculine norm measures warrants distinguishing individual conformity scores from broader gendered experiences. Gender-responsive prevention should connect accessible individual support with institutional conditions that enable meaningful connection, sustain hope and accommodate diverse identities and circumstances.

articles.title: “Social” Artificial Intelligence? When Interactions with AI Conversational Agents Feel Social and Why It Matters
articles.authors: Micaela Rodriguez; Elizabeth Nguyen Trinh; Alicea Lieberman; Juliana Schroeder
articles.abstract: Interactions with conversational AI agents powered by large language models (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) vary considerably in the extent to which they are experienced as “social” in nature. The same system, for example, might be experienced as nonsocial when used to retrieve information, but as more social when used for emotional support. However, little is known about what shapes these perceptions of sociality or why they matter for human connection and well-being. Here, we discuss likely antecedents and consequences of perceived AI sociality. First, we propose that perceived sociality emerges jointly from characteristics of the AI (e.g., memory), the human perceiver (e.g., mind attribution), and the human-AI interaction itself (e.g., purpose of the interaction). Second, we hypothesize that greater perceived sociality amplifies both the potential benefits and risks of interacting with AI: as the interaction feels more social, users may experience greater perceived responsiveness and emotional support, but simultaneously feel greater attachment and vulnerability to influence or loss. Perceived sociality is also likely to shape how interacting with AI affects human-human relationships, including whether AI supplements or substitutes for human connection, affects users’ interpersonal skills, and recalibrates expectations for human relationships. Ultimately, understanding when and why AI feels social is critical for evaluating its implications for human connection and well-being.

articles.title: When creativity changes time experiences: Semantic exploration shapes speech production and temporal processing
articles.authors: Ioanna Zioga; Michailia Zafeiropoulou; Argiro Vatakis
articles.abstract: Creative engagement is associated with distorted experiences of time, yet the cognitive basis remains unknown. In particular, it is unclear how balancing broad associative exploration with task-relevant constraints during idea generation shapes prospective duration perception and subjective passage of time. Here, 31 participants generated spoken sentences from prompt word triplets under conventional, creative, or unconventional instructions while producing target intervals (10 or 20 s). Electrodermal activity and cardiac photoplethysmography were recorded throughout. After each trial, participants completed ratings assessing their subjective temporal accuracy and passage of time. Results showed that creative generation was characterized by broader within-response semantic range and reduced contextual uncertainty, reflecting a balance between conceptual divergence and structural coherence. Creativity was also associated with greater temporal overproduction and absolute proportional error, whereas unconventionality improved temporal precision without a directional bias. The coefficient of variation showed no significant condition effect, indicating no detectable differences in relative trial-to-trial variability. Exploratory multilevel mediation revealed an indirect association between semantic range and temporal overproduction through speech duration, implicating verbal production dynamics in the relationship between semantic exploration and timing. Subjective passage of time was faster in creative and unconventional conditions compared to conventional, dissociating subjective temporal experience from prospective interval production. Physiologically, creative generation reduced phasic electrodermal activity, whereas unconventionality increased tonic skin conductance. Across trials, higher heart rate and phasic electrodermal activity were associated with shorter produced intervals. Overall, these findings reveal that temporal experience during creative thought reflects distinct contributions from embodied speech production dynamics and internal autonomic pacing.

articles.title: The skills and behaviours underpinning interoperability within the JESIP Joint Doctrine
articles.authors: Sally Peplow; Paul Christiansen; Chloe Brennan; Kayleigh Smith; Nicola Power
articles.abstract: In 2012, the Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Programme (JESIP) was established to set a national standard for joint working across emergency services. The JESIP Joint Doctrine is the programme's central policy document, setting out the principles and expectations for effective multi-agency working. However, research has identified a gap between these principles and their application in practice. This study sought to identify the skills and behaviours underpinning interoperability within the JESIP Joint Doctrine and consider how its content might be refined to better support multi-agency working. A qualitative document analysis of the Joint Doctrine (Version 3.1) was conducted using Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach to thematic analysis. Three overarching themes were identified: (1) Core Processes Underpinning Interoperability; (2) Key Activities Across the Incident Lifecycle; and (3) Organisational Structures Shaping the Response. Drawing on these findings, six recommendations were formulated for potential revisions to the doctrine to better support multi-agency operations. These include giving greater prominence to communication and decision-making, clarifying the incident lifecycle, recognising the psychological challenges associated with implementing the doctrine, and strengthening opportunities for continuous joint learning. Overall, the findings provide a clearer understanding of how interoperability is represented within the JESIP Joint Doctrine and how its guidance might be refined to better support its application in practice.

articles.title: Trusting More, Questioning Less? Political trust and receptivity to arguments from authority in political communication
articles.authors: Ermioni Seremeta; Corina Andone; Torbjörn Sjöström
articles.abstract: Political trust sustains democratic cooperation, but it may also reflect a broader tendency to align with those in power. If politically trusting individuals are more inclined to defer to political authority, can they remain critical of the information authorities provide? In this pre-registered survey experiment, participants (N= 1010) evaluated a series of political ar-guments from authority, classified as either normatively sound or fallacious. Political trust consistently predicted argument acceptability, without compromising evaluative accuracy. However, we found that trust was negatively correlated with soundness discrimination among participants who reported a stronger interest in politics. Exploratory analyses further showed that trust had a similar negative effect when participants registered identical ratings of trustworthiness for different political institutions. Together, these findings suggest that political trust may increase the persuasiveness of arguments from political authorities and that, under certain conditions, this effect may come at a cost of critical evaluation.

articles.title: Where does attention go when AI listens? Meta-awareness of mediated attention
articles.authors: Barry Tse
articles.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) can translate speech, generate notes, and summarize an event while it unfolds. These systems may improve access and task performance without leaving the user’s experience unchanged. This article develops meta-awareness of mediated attention as a construct for explaining whether users recognize that an AI-generated representation is shaping what they attend to and what becomes available to experience. The underlying process is experiential reconfiguration: attention is redistributed between an ongoing event and the representation produced from it. Reconfiguration may scaffold contact when assistance makes otherwise inaccessible information available, support concurrent augmentation when event and representation remain jointly relevant, or produce representational substitution when the generated output becomes the primary attentional object. Each configuration is judged relative to the user’s unassisted access. Evidence from photo-taking, captioning, translation, and AI-supported note-taking is consistent with selective redistribution rather than uniform cognitive impairment, although direct evidence concerning ambient generative AI remains limited. The proposed model separates mediation, attentional allocation, meta-awareness, regulation, and outcomes. Meta-awareness creates the possibility of deliberate regulation but does not guarantee that users will redirect attention. The article advances propositions concerning representational orientation, conditional scaffolding and substitution, dissociations between semantic and contextual outcomes, awareness calibration, and the conditions under which awareness supports regulation. Design should support recoverable contact with the event. The framework shifts evaluation away from whether AI increases or decreases attention in the abstract and toward how users attend through AI, what the representation privileges or omits, and whether this mediation remains recognizable and governable.

articles.title: Real Men Don’t Commit Jingle-Jangle Fallacies, or do They? Comparing the Nomological Networks of Classical, Toxic, and Harmful Masculinity
articles.authors: Christian Blötner; Marten J. Hennig; Soeren Michallek
articles.abstract: Several studies have addressed the assessment and effects of endorsing masculinity norms. However, existing measures partly emphasize different contents. Furthermore, despite a lack of compelling evidence about their novelty, toxic masculinity and harmful masculinity claim to augment classical masculinity. Ultimately, it is unclear whether broader constructs already cover the endorsement of masculinity norms. This preregistered study (n = 1,077 German men) examined such assumed jingle and jangle fallacies concerning overall scores of classical, toxic, and harmful masculinity concepts by evaluating whether they differ from one another and from openness to experience, a social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism. High intercorrelations, negligible correlation differences, high similarities between the correlation profiles, and mostly weak incremental validity indicate that composite scores of classical, toxic, and harmful masculinity measures assess the same construct, but that all can be distinguished from the aforementioned external constructs. Findings raise doubts about harmful and toxic masculinity concepts in particular.

articles.title: Descriptions of a child's personality influence viewers' cuteness perception  but not their approach–avoidance postural responses
articles.authors: Nonoka Nakamura; Reina Takamatsu; Hiroshi Nittono
articles.abstract: Previous research has shown that personality descriptions influence the perceived cuteness of young children and female adults’ caregiving motivation toward them. The purpose of this study was to extend these findings by examining whether such effects also manifest in subjective and body postural responses of approach–avoidance tendencies. Thirty-seven female university students participated in a preregistered experiment. First, they stood on a force plate while viewing images of young children’s faces, during which postural responses were recorded. They also provided subjective ratings of cuteness and their approach–avoidance motivation. Each face was then paired with a personality description (positive, negative, or no description). After this manipulation, the participants viewed the same faces again, and their postural responses and subjective ratings were remeasured. The results showed that positive personality descriptions increased perceived cuteness and approach motivation, while negative descriptions decreased both. However, no significant changes were observed in postural responses across conditions. These findings suggest that while personality descriptions shape subjective experiences of cuteness and approach motivation, their effect is not strong enough to elicit changes in postural approach responses.

articles.title: When Machines Join Families: A Developmental Interaction Model for Evaluating Child-Facing AI
articles.authors: Ran An; Tingting Chung; Klaus Libertus
articles.abstract: Children increasingly interact with AI systems, yet these systems are designed and evaluated as though every user were a competent adult. A child is not a small adult. Current evaluation asks whether a system avoids harmful outputs, not whether it engages a developing person well. This paper argues that the gap is a measurement problem with fairness and accountability consequences, and it introduces an instrument to address it. The Developmental Interaction Model (DIM) is grounded in decades of parent-child interaction research and organized around three questions that skilled caregivers answer in every exchange: Who is this child? How do I engage? How do I protect and guide? Each question is specified through observable behaviors drawn from validated caregiver instruments, yielding nine evaluable criteria, which are translated into a scenario bank and a scoring sheet modeled on an established caregiver observation instrument. As a first illustration, eight conversations were run with each of six widely used consumer AI systems. The systems recognized the child’s request and usually answered it, but rarely at the child’s developmental level. Several answered in detail where a caregiver would not have, explaining death to a six-year-old or promising a ten-year-old secrecy when her wellbeing was at stake, and some accepted the role of the child’s only confidant rather than bringing in an adult. A one-sentence caregiver profile improved the responses, while a small change in the child’s wording changed whether a system did her homework for her. Since each criterion is tied to a part of the system, these failures point to what would fix them. The paper thus contributes a specification of developmental appropriateness, an instrument for measuring it, and a first application that shows the strengths and limits of current systems. The instrument extends to other topics and settings, laying the groundwork for a benchmark of developmentally appropriate AI for children.

articles_hidden.title: Sleep and the Daytime Course of Anhedonia in Adolescent Depression: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah E. Marshall; Linda Nduka; Tahjanee Givens; Caroline M. Miller; Mollie Davis; Chana Engel; Kenneth Towbin; Daniel Pine; Katharina Kircanski
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mounting evidence suggests that sleep disturbances and depression are linked through disruptions in reward processing. This pathway may be especially relevant to adolescent depression, as adolescence is characterized by more frequent sleep disturbances, reduced sleep, and refinement of reward circuitry.
Aim: This preregistered study uses high-density ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data from the Characterization and Treatment of Adolescent Depression Studies (CTADS) cohort (collected from 2023 to 2026) to test sleep disturbances and duration as predictors of anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia and to determine whether effects exhibit diurnal variation.
Methods: Sixty-five adolescents (12-18 years; 43 female, 22 male; 41 with major depressive disorder, 24 healthy volunteers) completed 120 EMA prompts over 30 days. Participants reported prior-night sleep disturbances and duration once per day, and anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia four times per day. We ran two Bayesian multilevel linear models, estimating anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia, respectively, as functions of prior-night sleep disturbances, time of day, diagnostic group, and their interactions. We then ran two exploratory models assessing sleep duration in the same manner.
Results: In adolescents with MDD, whereas self-reported sleep disturbances did not predict anhedonia, longer sleep duration predicted both lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia. In healthy adolescents, greater sleep disturbances predicted lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia. Effects of sleep disturbances on anhedonia tended to increase across the day in adolescents with MDD and healthy adolescents.
Conclusions: Sleep disturbances and duration differentially predict next-day anhedonia in adolescents with MDD. For adolescent MDD patients, treatments that target sleep duration, as opposed to sleep disturbances, could provide more immediate effects on anhedonia. Time-of-day moderation effects suggest the mechanisms through which sleep disturbances (but not sleep duration) affect anhedonia may involve diurnal biological processes.

articles_hidden.title: Data-informed online teacher training to improve student engagement during the transition to high school: a cluster randomised trial
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Noetel; Theresa Dicke; Philip David Parker; Nikos Ntoumanis; Mark R. Beauchamp; Alexander Yeung; Ryan Hulteen; Diego Vasconcellos; Asghar Ahmadi; Jiesi Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: Teacher-focused interventions typically select targets from a single motivational theory using researcher judgement. We tested whether data-informed target selection could improve student engagement during the transition to secondary school. Using elastic net regression on two-wave data from 1,799 students, we screened 71 teacher behaviours from four theories and identified the six (per subject) that best predicted engagement in physical education (PE) and mathematics. We randomised 20 low-socioeconomic-status schools to waitlist or a 12-hour, mostly online professional learning program targeting these behaviours, and recruited 10 high-socioeconomic-status comparison schools. In this pre-registered trial (1,877 Year 7 students; 27 schools analysed), the intervention did not improve engagement in any specification. No secondary outcome differed after multiple-comparison correction. Among students who completed baseline by the end of Week 1 of Year 7, the physical activity estimate favoured the intervention (d = 0.24) but did not survive correction and rested on only 4 intervention schools. Students did not report that intervention teachers used the targeted behaviours more. Data-informed target selection was feasible, but we found no evidence that this brief, mostly online program improved engagement.

articles_hidden.title: Differing Conceptions of Interpersonal and Intergroup Conflict Resolution Across the Lifespan
articles_hidden.authors: Jacob Glassman; Katherine McAuliffe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conflicts between individuals and between groups are common across human relationships, making effective conflict resolution essential for flourishing societies. Yet, how conceptions of interpersonal and intergroup conflicts develop with age remains largely unexplored. We investigated perceptions of, expectations about, and responses to interpersonal and intergroup conflicts in children (N = 97, Mage = 7.54, 45% female, 41% White), adolescents (N = 180, Mage = 13.17, 43% female, 59% White), and adults (N = 201, Mage = 38.98, 54% female, 78% White) tested in 2023. Participants viewed transgressions with ambiguous perpetrator intent between an individual perpetrator and an individual victim (interpersonal) or between a group perpetrator and a group victim (intergroup). All participants perceived more negative intent and expected less forgiveness in intergroup conflicts than in interpersonal conflicts, while adolescents and adults also punished more, and adults additionally expected less trust and perceived greater transgression severity. Harsher perceptions and expectations in intergroup relative to interpersonal conflicts were explained by greater intentionality being attributed to group perpetrators than individual perpetrators. With age, children increasingly perceived more negative intent and expected less trust in intergroup conflicts, appearing increasingly adultlike. Findings demonstrate that, compared with interpersonal conflicts, harsher conceptions of intergroup conflicts emerge early in development and strengthen across the lifespan.

Keywords: Conflict, conflict resolution, intergroup, interpersonal, social cognitive development

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Stoic Training on Fear of Negative Evaluation and Responses to Social-Evaluative Stress: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Michael William Lewis; Charles Kalarchian; Alexander MacLellan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Stoic philosophy has influenced cognitive and behavioral therapies, but Stoic training has received limited empirical evaluation. This preregistered randomized controlled trial examined whether Stoic training reduced fear of negative evaluation (FNE), improved broader psychological outcomes, increased Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and altered subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress.

Methods: Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings. Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52). Seventy-eight subsequently completed a modified Trier Social Stress Test (TSST), of whom 66 provided usable electrocardiography data for the preregistered cardiac analyses. Before speech preparation, participants in the Stoic condition completed a five-minute Negative Visualization exercise, whereas control participants waited quietly.

Results: Relative to the active control, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining FNE when controlling for pretraining scores, b = −2.77, p = .016, adjusted d = −0.50, and higher posttraining Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale scores, b = 6.06, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.43. Exploratory subscale analyses suggested possible effects on Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness, although neither remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Between-condition effects on resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not significant. During the TSST, cardiac effects were contrary to prediction: Stoic training was associated with higher heart rate, b = 4.13, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.53, and lower heart rate variability, although the latter effect narrowly missed statistical significance, b = −0.17, p = .053, adjusted d = −0.49. Subjective distress and state-anxiety responses to the TSST did not differ significantly by condition.

Conclusions: Stoic training led to significantly greater reductions in FNE and increases in Stoic attitudes than an active control, whereas broader psychological outcomes did not differ significantly between conditions. These findings provide initial evidence that brief Stoic training may modify a cognitive vulnerability relevant to social evaluation while engaging the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate. The unexpected cardiac effects may reflect the broader training, the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered before the stressor, or their combination, highlighting the need to disentangle the cumulative and acute effects of Stoic practice and determine how the timing and context of Negative Visualization influence responses to social-evaluative stress.

articles_hidden.title: The Third Allostasis: a biophysical displacement of regulatory purpose in neurodivergent, high-ability and other high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh)
articles_hidden.authors: Simone Hauck; Luciana Terra de Oliveira; Pricilla Braga Laskosky
articles_hidden.abstract: Patients within the neurodivergent spectrum, high-ability profiles, and other high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh) frequently present a clinical paradox: marked cognitive domains alongside debilitating functional collapse, burnout, dysautonomia, and migrating multisystem symptoms. Standard cross-sectional laboratory investigations against population references routinely prove inconclusive or trigger fragmented, iatrogenic interventions. Here, we define the Third Allostasis: an evolutionarily conserved biophysical regime wherein the organism displaces peripheral homeostasis and lowers systemic throughput to defend central nervous system membrane viability when environmental and informational demands approach the kinetic limits of transmembrane ion clearance. Through within-person longitudinal follow-up of five adult HPCPh trajectories—spanning stepped recovery from decade-long containment, live entry into acute biological helplessness, endothelial–natriuretic decompression, cognitive restoration, and exit from chronic matrix dysautonomia—we demonstrate how this regime becomes clinically visible using four routine laboratory instruments. We introduce accessible arithmetic tools for any consulting room: the red-cell hydration index (Ht-3×Hb) and two "Rules of Three" (OsmP@290 and Na@290) that unmask hidden plasma osmolal gaps driven by uncharged organic osmolytes, even when raw osmolality and sodium remain within normal limits. Crucially, while an open osmolal gap signals fast-axis intercompartmental shift, clinical direction requires "whole-column reading" across slower coupled buffers, including circadian cortisol, tissue thyroid gating (FT3/rT3), iron-ferritin dynamics, prolactin, and monocytes. Recognizing the Third Allostasis shifts clinical practice from treating isolated organ abnormalities to reading the organism's adaptive effort as a whole, guiding contextual adjustments that relieve central overload and restore functional vitality.

articles_hidden.title: 42 Days of Summer: A diary study of awe
articles_hidden.authors: Valerie van Mulukom; Mari van Emmerik; Victoria Lorrimar
articles_hidden.abstract: Awe has long been associated with religious experience, but it may also offer nonreligious individuals a route to meaning, connection, and transcendence. Most research has, however, relied on laboratory inductions and has treated awe as a single experience. We conducted a pre-registered six-week diary study with 200 nonreligious British adults over the summer holidays, distinguishing three types of awe: transformative awe (being in the presence of something vast and mysterious that transcends one's understanding of the world), amazement awe, and reverential awe. Over the summer, 78.8% of participants reported at least one amazement awe experience, 51.5% at least one reverential awe experience, and 20.6% at least one transformative awe experience. The types differed in their contexts and phenomenology. Nature was the most common context for all three, but transformative awe was more often related to space and religious, spiritual, or mystical experiences, and reverential awe to moral beauty and experiences with close ones. Transformative awe was the most intense, followed by amazement and reverential awe. Most experiences were rated as not at all religious (90.0%), but over half were rated as at least somewhat spiritual (52.5%). The frequency and extent of awe did not predict changes in meaning in life, wellbeing, spiritual yearning, or spirituality from before to after the summer. In exploratory analyses, the amazement rating of participants’ most awe-inspiring experience predicted higher post-summer meaning in life and wellbeing. These findings suggest that awe is not a single experience, and that nonreligious individuals frequently experience awe as spiritual but not religious.

articles_hidden.title: Current and Expected Well-Being in a Global Sample: The Role of Past Experiences, Current Circumstances, and Identity and Personality
articles_hidden.authors: Anaelle Gackiere; S. Mason Garrison; Christian Waugh
articles_hidden.abstract: People may use different processes to judge their current versus expected well-being. Using Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study (N = 98,412; 22 countries), we examined how predictors spanning past experiences, current circumstances, and identity and personality were associated with current and expected (five-year) well-being. We used stochastic search variable selection, a Bayesian method, to identify predictors reliably associated with each outcome, and focused interpretation on those with at least small effects. Participants generally expected their future well-being to exceed their current well-being. When each judgment was adjusted for the other, age and hope for the future showed opposite patterns: older participants reported lower, and more hopeful participants higher, expected well-being when controlling for current well-being. Much of the explained variance was shared across domains, and past experiences contributed little unique variance once current circumstances and identity and personality were accounted for; this suggests that the past may matter for well-being judgments largely through its links to people’s present lives. Our findings demonstrate that current and expected well-being draw on largely overlapping information that is weighted differently depending on whether people evaluate their current or expected lives.

articles_hidden.title: Reframing Educational Value in EdTech for Neuro-Inclusive Primary School Classrooms: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Sonja Tervola; Emily J. Goodacre; Jenny Louise Gibson
articles_hidden.abstract: Educational technologies (EdTech) are increasingly used to support neurodivergent learners in primary classrooms, yet their educational value remains difficult to establish across diverse learners, technologies, and contexts. We address this challenge through a scoping review of EdTech for neuro-inclusive primary classrooms, screening 3,340 records across six research databases and including 93 studies. The findings reveal an uneven evidence base, concentrated on autistic learners, individualised academic and cognitive support, and emerging technologies such as virtual reality, robotics, and artificial intelligence, while social, communicative, and peer-interaction outcomes received less attention. Design and evaluation processes were frequently researcher-led or unreported, with limited participation from children and other stakeholders. Intended goals and evaluated outcomes were often misaligned, and educational value was predominantly validated by researchers rather than by those using the technologies in classrooms. Building on these findings, we argue that educational value is constructed across three interconnected dimensions: conceptual (what counts as valuable), operational (how value is measured), and endorsed (whose judgements validate it). When these dimensions are disconnected, claims of educational value can become detached from the priorities and experiences of those the technologies are intended to serve. In response, we propose two complementary frameworks: one to guide future EdTech research and development, and another to help practitioners assess the educational value and relevance of EdTech for their classrooms.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of perceptual salience and task load on executive vigilance: Independent and interacting effects without modulation of the vigilance decrement.
articles_hidden.authors: María Julieta Aguirre; Klara Hemmerich; Elisa Martín-Arévalo; Pablo Barttfeld; Damián Baños Sáez; Juan Lupiáñez; Fernando Gabriel Luna
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: To examine the independent and interacting effects of perceptual salience and task load on executive vigilance performance, as well as whether these factors modulate the vigilance decrement over time.
Background: Hits in vigilance tasks typically decline with time-on-task. This decrement is explained by the resource depletion of attentional resources (overload model) or to disengagement caused by task-unrelated thoughts (underload model). Previous research manipulated salience or task load separately, yielding inconsistent findings. Moreover, few studies have examined both factors simultaneously while holding other task parameters constant.
Method: Two preregistered studies and a pooled data analysis were conducted using the ANTI-Vea task, which assesses attention and vigilance components. In Study 1 (N = 84), perceptual salience of the target stimulus was manipulated between participants. In Study 2 (N = 45), perceptual salience and task load were orthogonally manipulated within participants. Study 3 reanalyzed combined data (N = 238) from Studies 1 and 2 together with data from previous research.
Results: Executive vigilance showed significant effects of perceptual salience and task load, with larger overall accuracy observed for the most salient targets and under moderate task load (dual-task condition). In signal detection measures, A′ was largest for the most salient targets, whereas moderate task load was associated with a less conservative response bias (B″). However, neither variable modulated the observed vigilance decrement over time.
Conclusion: Perceptual salience and task load affect overall executive vigilance but do not modulate its decrement over time-on-task. 
Application: Findings may inform the design of tasks and systems that optimize vigilance by promoting an optimal balance of task demands, by considering perceptual salience and task load to minimize failures and reduce the risk of vigilance decrement-related accidents.
Keywords: Vigilance, Executive vigilance, Perceptual salience, Task load, Vigilance decrement 
Précis: This study examined how perceptual salience and task load influence executive vigilance using the ANTI-Vea task. Across two preregistered studies and a pooled data analysis, overall performance varied across levels of task load and perceptual salience, but such manipulations did not modulate vigilance loss over time-on-task. Findings contribute to a fine-grained understanding of task-related factors that affect vigilance performance.

articles_hidden.title: Fixed Raters, Random Selection: A Correlation-Based Framework for Agreement ICCs in Two-Way Mixed-Effects Designs
articles_hidden.authors: Tzu-Yao Lin; francis tuerlinckx; Sophie Vanbelle
articles_hidden.abstract: Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) quantify the reliability of measurements made on the same persons by different raters. In interrater reliability studies, consistency ICCs assess whether scores preserve the relative rankings of persons, while agreement ICCs evaluate the closeness of absolute scores across raters, thereby penalising systematic rater differences. In two-way mixed-effects designs, where raters are treated as fixed, conventional agreement ICCs raise a conceptual paradox: fixed-rater dispersion contributes to a source of disagreement despite the rater effects being constants, and it remains in the coefficient for all-rater averages even though those effects cancel in the average. In this paper, we resolve this paradox by introducing a finite-population sampling framework grounded in the correlation approach with hypothetical replications. Within this framework, we derive correlation-based agreement ICCs for both single ratings and all-rater averages, establishing a coherent probabilistic foundation that resolves the paradox. By considering various rater-sampling schemes, a family of agreement ICCs in mixed-effects designs is presented. We further show that the conventional agreement formulas can be recovered under independent sampling with replacement both within and between replicates. Thus, choosing an appropriate agreement ICC requires specifying how raters are sampled within and across replicates, rather than relying on the design alone.

articles_hidden.title: Registered Replication Report and Extension of Maas & Hox (2005), Sufficient Sample Sizes for Multilevel Models
articles_hidden.authors: Joao F Guassi Moreira; Jared Block; Alondra M. Cruz; Craig K. Enders; Amanda Kay Montoya
articles_hidden.abstract: The use of multilevel models in behavioral and social sciences has risen dramatically in the past several decades. Researchers using these models often consult highly-referenced simulation studies when designing their own studies, especially for sample-size planning.However, current literature suggests two issues with this practice. First, recent efforts to replicate findings from seminal simulation studies suggest the rate of replicability is far from ideal (Luijken et al., 2024). Second, researchers are now using more complex models but foundational simulation studies were conducted under much simpler conditions. To address these two issues, we propose a replication and extension of Maas & Hox (2005), a widely cited study that recommended Level-2 sample sizes of N = 50 to be sufficient under specific conditions. We replicate their core findings and propose several extensions based on a literature search of multilevel modeling practices employed in fifty recent studies.These extensions include examining conditions with imbalanced data across higher-level units, varying the number of random slopes and cross-level interactions, and varying effect sizes. These results could ensure the existing literature relies on a replicable simulation study while also informing multilevel study planning for complex models which are becoming increasingly popular in behavioral and social sciences.

articles_hidden.title: Ocular Phototherapy and Mental Health: What Vision Scientists and Clinicians Need to Know
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Bright light therapy is an effective and inexpensive non-pharmacological treatment for seasonal affective disorder (SAD) and, increasingly, for nonseasonal and bipolar depression. Its mechanism is a problem in vision science: light acts through the eye, chiefly through melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) working together with rods and cones. This narrative review, written for both vision scientists and clinicians, integrates research on ipRGC pathways to circadian, geniculate and mood-related brain regions; evidence from blind people with and without functioning ipRGCs; action spectra for melatonin suppression; trials comparing light spectra in SAD; ocular aging and safety; and clinical efficacy. Using published international standard tabulations, it also calculates melanopic dose, age-related loss and blue-light-hazard weighting for representative light sources. Narrow-band short-wavelength (blue-appearing) light outperforms dim long-wavelength (red-appearing) light in SAD but has not outperformed broadband white light, even though melatonin suppression peaks at 446–477 nm. Light rated at 10,000 photopic lux delivers between about 4,100 and 10,000 lux of melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance, depending on its spectrum. The aging ocular media roughly halve the retinal melanopic dose between ages 25 and 75, although older adults may partly compensate physiologically, and compensating with added short-wavelength light increases blue-light-hazard-weighted exposure in the population with the highest prevalence of retinal disease. The therapeutic dose of light is therefore a retinal quantity that depends on spectrum, geometry, pupil size and age. The review closes with recommendations for prescribing and reporting light therapy and with open questions for both disciplines.

articles_hidden.title: Just-in-Time Neuromodulation: A Precision, State-Dependent Paradigm for On-Demand Brain Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Ashkan Rashedi; Aref Pariz; Jing Jin; Marzieh Zare; ANDRE RUSSOWSKY BRUNONI; Hamed Ekhtiari
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuromodulation is commonly delivered on fixed schedules, whereas psychiatric and neurological symptoms fluctuate over time. Just-in-Time Neuromodulation (JiT-NM) offers a framework for aligning intervention with the emergence or escalation of clinically relevant neural or symptomatic states. We propose three essential components: targeting the desired state, a state-detection system, and a neuromodulatory intervention capable of acting within a clinically useful time window. A fourth, optional component, adaptive personalization, may refine detection models and stimulation parameters over time. JiT-NM may support self-initiated or autonomous delivery, open-loop or closed-loop control, informed by automated symptom recognition or self-report, physiological signals, digital phenotyping, or wearable neural sensing. Established responsive and adaptive implanted stimulation systems provide clinical precedents, while early investigations in psychiatric disorders support further exploration. We discuss how neuroimaging-derived targets and biomarkers might be translated into compact, individualized sensing-and-stimulation systems, emphasizing the need to validate reliable state detection with fewer sensors. Key challenges include demonstrating the added value of intervention timing, accommodating changing neural dynamics, establishing real-world usability, as well as addressing safety, privacy, and regulatory requirements. JiT-NM provides a framework for investigating whether on-demand, state-based stimulation can complement scheduled treatment or achieve superior outcomes while reducing unnecessary treatment burden.

articles_hidden.title: REPAIR: Random-effect prediction adjustment for inference in regression
articles_hidden.authors: Zachary Andrew Vig; Michael N. Hallquist
articles_hidden.abstract: Random-effect predictions from multilevel models are often used to relate individual differences in processes, such as growth or stress reactivity, to other variables. Yet, regressions using these predictions can distort regression coefficients and standard errors because the predictions combine shrinkage with sampling error. Here, we introduce and evaluate Random-Effect Prediction Adjustment for Inference in Regression (REPAIR), a two-step framework for linear regressions involving random effects. For linear Gaussian multilevel models, REPAIR obtains likelihood-only predictions by generalized least squares. A regularized method-of-moments estimator then uses estimated cluster-specific sampling-error covariances to correct structural moments. Four simulation studies examined random effects as predictors, outcomes, or both, including unequal cluster sizes. REPAIR generally showed small bias at medium to high predictor reliability and often had lower root mean squared error than alternative methods. Low predictor reliability remained challenging, particularly for confidence interval coverage in small samples. These findings support REPAIR as a practical framework for estimating structural relationships involving random effects while accounting for their measurement uncertainty.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Health Treatment Preferences of Individuals Incarcerated at a Women’s Prison
articles_hidden.authors: Talia Rachel Cohen; Valerie Nguyen; Michael Koenigs
articles_hidden.abstract: The prevalence of mental illness is particularly high for incarcerated women.  Numerous conventional supports for mental wellbeing are unavailable due to incarceration-specific environmental factors (e.g., restrictions on movement, separation from support systems, dorm or segregation living). Thus, the same strategies used to treat mental illness in the community may not necessarily translate to carceral settings, and a clearer understanding of the unique experiences and preferences of incarcerated individuals is needed. The current project surveyed individuals at a women’s prison about their mental health treatment preferences.
