Results showed high favorability for mental health treatment across the board, with the highest ratings for self-administered treatment options. Participants also preferred Department of Corrections (DOC) providers to peer providers and individual support to group support. Clinical considerations for the DOC are discussed, including prioritizing confidentiality, investing in self-administered options, incorporating individualized elements into group programming, and using preference surveys to inform resource allocation.

articles_hidden.title: Young Life Evaluation in Decline: A Case Study of Norway
articles_hidden.authors: August Nilsson; Karoline Kopperud; Espen Røysamb; Tim Lomas; Lyle H Ungar; Ragnhild Bang Nes
articles_hidden.abstract: In 73% of the world’s countries, adults under 30 years of age report the highest life evaluation (i.e., happiness). A notable exception has emerged in North America and Northern Europe, where this pattern has reversed, with older adults reporting greater life evaluation than the young. We analyzed Gallup World Poll data from 2006–2024, covering 2.6 million respondents worldwide and 16,009 in Norway, to examine shifts in the age gap in life evaluation and their determinants. Norway is a particularly valuable case for illustrating this reversal: since ranking as the world’s happiest country in 2017, it has declined in both absolute terms and relative rankings, with national statistics revealing a pronounced well-being gap between young and old. We found that the decline in life evaluation scores in Norway largely reflects decreasing scores among young adults (18-30 years), whose scores have dropped significantly since 2017 (p < .001; d = 0.37) and are now markedly lower than those of older adults (p < .001; d = 0.41). We further confirmed that this trend is limited to a small set of countries; of all 2,508 linear correlations between age and life evaluation in different countries, 83% were negative, and only 2% were r > .10, which was the case in Norway 2022–2024. We examined potential explanations of the observed change in Norway. Only a few of the 70 variables in the Gallup World Poll seem potentially relevant for the increased age difference in life evaluations in Norway. Across multiple analyses we find the most important variables are i) stress-related factors (e.g., feeling well-rested and stress), and ii) economic standards (e.g., standard of living satisfaction and household income satisfaction). The study emphasizes the imperative for highly developed countries to prioritise the well-being of their young despite overall prosperity and high living standards.

articles_hidden.title: Binding Memory and Relational Mechanisms: The Central Role of Binding in Fluid Intelligence
articles_hidden.authors: William Frederick Garvey; Alon Zivony; Alicia Forsberg; Claudia Christina von Bastian
articles_hidden.abstract: Fluid intelligence (Gf) and working memory (WM) are strongly correlated, with the binding hypothesis suggesting that this relationship is driven by the capacity to bind content to context. However, it remains unclear how various binding functions overlap and relate to Gf. This study investigates the extent of overlap between five binding functions (item-to-location binding, item-to-item binding, relational integration, relation processing, and perceptual feature binding) and their relationship with Gf. A sample of 174 young adults completed three visuospatial variants of tasks measuring these five binding functions alongside three Gf tasks. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling and latent network analysis to evaluate shared and unique variances. Results indicated significant overlap among the binding functions, with item-to-location and item-to-item binding best modeled as a single latent variable termed binding memory. The shared variance among binding memory and the remaining binding functions was represented by a higher-order, process-general latent factor labeled Binding which was found to be statistically isomorphic with Gf. Latent network analysis further revealed that binding memory, relational integration, and relation processing each exhibited unique, direct relationships with Gf, whereas perceptual feature binding related to Gf only indirectly. These findings indicate that an overarching, domain-general ability to form and utilize bindings in a goal-directed manner is deeply intertwined with Gf, supporting theories emphasizing binding and relational mechanisms in Gf.

articles_hidden.title: The Precision Trap: On the Idealization of Mathematics in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Sepehrdad Rahimian
articles_hidden.abstract: Calls for greater precision and mathematization in psychology are often motivated by the hope that they will help overcome the field's theoretical problems. While mathematics undoubtedly contributes to scientific progress, this paper questions the idea that an increase in mathematization, in itself, constitutes progress. First, it examines the tradeoffs of precision, arguing that making a theory more precise can change what is being studied, reduce its functionality, and sometimes lend an unwarranted authority to its claims. It also considers examples of non-mathematical yet successful psychological approaches. Second, the paper introduces the Mathematization Bind. Under a realist standard, mathematical precision cannot, by itself, establish that a theory has moved closer to Reality, as the history of the luminiferous aether illustrates. Under a pragmatic standard, the value of mathematics depends on what it enables us to accomplish, relative to the goals of inquiry. Neither perspective justifies treating greater mathematization as scientific progress by default. The paper also questions the tendency to regard an idealized image of physics as the model of scientific maturity. It concludes that the appropriate role and degree of mathematization in psychology should be determined by what it actually contributes to scientific inquiry, rather than by expectations about what a mature science ought to look like.

articles_hidden.title: When One Random Effect Is Not Enough: Mixture Model Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Caspar J. Van Lissa
articles_hidden.abstract: Handling between-study differences in effect sizes, or heterogeneity, is a key challenge in meta-analysis.  The common assumption that heterogeneity is normally distributed implies an absence of systematic sources of heterogeneity, or known and measured sources of heterogeneity that can be controlled using moderator analysis.  These assumptions fall short when effect sizes originate from multiple unknown subpopulations - for example, due to different research traditions, unmeasured moderators, publication bias, and outliers.  It has been argued that finite mixture models - also known as latent class analysis (LCA) - can capture these unobserved subgroups,  but there is currently no generalized framework for estimating such models.  We introduce open source software for estimating random-effects mixture, or "remix" meta-analyses.  Implemented in `OpenMx`, these structural equation models can be fully customized and further extended.  We conducted a simulation study to evaluate the `remix` algorithm's convergence, bias and confidence interval coverage,  and the performance of several class enumeration metrics: the AIC, BIC, and ICL information criteria, predictive model comparison (PMC), and cross-validation.  Results show that the method is fast and has low bias, but confidence interval coverage is below nominal levels,  and class enumeration remains challenging - which are known limitations of LCA.  Nevertheless, remix meta-analysis is the appropriate method when effect sizes originate from a mixture of unobserved subpopulations; a scenario which is arguably commonplace in meta-analysis.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping Altered Temporality: Human-Validated LLM Analysis of Naturalistic Trip Reports
articles_hidden.authors: Paweł Gładziejewski; Aleksander Milczanowski; Bogna Bylicka; Jan Nikadon
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychedelic substances can profoundly alter the experience of time, yet we lack a detailed account of which distinct temporal alterations occur, how prevalent they are, and how they are interrelated. A key obstacle is that the methods best suited to capturing the phenomenological repertoire of altered temporality are difficult to scale and may therefore fail to reliably capture rare phenomena, whereas scalable psychometric tools lack the categorical resolution to tease apart distinct types of experience. Here we combine resolution with scale, applying a theorist-constructed phenomenological codebook to naturalistic psychedelic trip reports through large language model (LLM)-based, corpus-scale content analysis. First, we establish that altered temporality resolves into seven textually distinguishable categories, recovered with similar reliability by human and LLM coders. Second, we apply LLM-based qualitative analysis to 3,291 excerpts from a corpus of 7,303 psychedelic trip reports, confirming that this categorical structure holds at corpus scale. Third, we estimate category prevalence and identify a stable associative structure comprising a complex of rare, interconnected alterations centered on timelessness and metaphysical appraisals, alongside an independent, more prevalent alteration in the subjective rate and duration of temporal flow. Fourth, we show that a similar relative prevalence profile and broad associative pattern, derived from the English-language Shroomery corpus, replicate in the independent Polish-language Neurogroove repository. Our study provides a high-resolution map of psychedelic temporality, arrived at by a method that may generalize beyond it, toward recovering the taxonomic structure of altered states of consciousness.

articles_hidden.title: Reciprocal Associations Between Cannabis Initiation and  Recurrent Binge Eating Onset in US Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Kavish Chapra; Ya-Wen Chang; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Cannabis use and binge eating often co-occur; however, the order and timing of their onset are not well described in population-based samples, limiting our understanding of potential risk pathways between the two behaviors. 

Method: We examined the order and timing of onset of these behaviors among 12,314 adults from the Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys. Cannabis initiation and recurrent binge eating (i.e., binge eating at least twice weekly for 3 months) were dated using ages of onset reported at a single interview. Survey-weighted survival and discrete-time models estimated cumulative probabilities and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for onset of each behavior after the other. 

Results: Among 251 adults reporting both behaviors, cannabis initiation came first for 62.3% (95% CI [52.9, 71.7]) and binge eating came first for 33.2% (95% CI [23.8, 42.5]). The median interval between behaviors was 4 to 5 years. Within 10 years of cannabis initiation, 2.6% (95% CI [1.7, 3.6]) had reported binge eating onset; in contrast, within 10 years of binge eating onset, 35.6% (95% CI [24.7, 45.0]) had reported cannabis initiation. Prior cannabis initiation was associated with higher annual odds of binge eating onset (OR = 2.23, 95% CI [1.46, 3.39], p < .001), and prior binge eating was associated with higher annual odds of cannabis initiation (OR = 1.61, 95% CI [1.07, 2.42], p = .024). In secondary analyses, the association of prior cannabis initiation with binge eating onset was significant among women (OR = 2.63, p < .001) but not men (OR = 1.81, p = .113). The sex interaction was not significant after correction (q = .063). 

Conclusions: Each behavior was associated with later onset of the other, suggesting a two-way association rather than a single direction of influence. Thus, clinicians treating either behavior should consider asking about the other. However, because onset ages were recalled, prospective research is critical to test causal direction.

articles_hidden.title: The Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker: Mental Sampling Processes Capture Preference, Confidence and Response Time in Risky Choice
articles_hidden.authors: Jake Spicer; Yun-Xiao Li; Lucas Castillo; Johanna Falben; Stella Qian; Adam N Sanborn
articles_hidden.abstract: Modern models of preferential decision making have achieved substantial success in predicting choice behaviour both qualitatively and quantitatively, but often overlook related aspects such as response time or confidence. In parallel, recently proposed mental sampling frameworks have offered broad explanations for multiple aspects of behaviour including probability judgments, perceptual estimates and numerical forecasts, but have not yet been applied to preferential choice. Here, we seek to unite these lines of research by extending one such framework, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS; Zhu et al., 2024), to decisions between alternatives which differ in the value of their potential outcomes. We present a new version of the ABS adapted to such decisions, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker (ABDM), able to predict not just choices, but also reaction times and confidence in selections. We compare the predictions of the ABDM against extant choice and response time data in risky choice tasks, finding strong correspondence in both. We also contrast the new model against leading explanations for behaviour in such tasks, showing the ABDM is competitive in choice and ahead in response times. We thus propose this model as a broader approach to decision making capable of explaining multiple measures from a common process.

articles_hidden.title: What Is a “Blank” Mind? Testing the Meaning and Construct Validity of Mind-Blanking Reports to Thought Probes
articles_hidden.authors: Chandni Lal; Matt Welhaf; Michael J. Kane
articles_hidden.abstract: Four studies evaluated probed mind-blanking reports, an off-task conscious state ostensibly experienced as an absence of thought and subjective experience. We examined whether people make mind-blanking reports to indicate uncertainty about their preceding thoughts, rather than to communicate an experienced “blank;” we also assessed whether subjects used “blank” to refer to the absence of experience, or rather an unclear, diffuse form of experience. U.S.-based Prolific participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that differed in thought-probe response options, which included or did not include “I-don’t-know” and “mind-blanking” options in Study 1a, 1b, and 2 (Ns = 463–790). Within an online go/no-go task, we tested whether different response options yielded different rates of mind-blanking and I-don’t-know reports. That is, would mind-blanking rates be higher when an “I don’t know” response option was not available, suggesting that mind-blanking reports indicate uncertainty? Would rates of I-don’t-know reports be lower when the “mind-blanking” option was unavailable? Neither mind-blanking nor I-don’t-know report rates differed significantly between probe-type conditions. Subjects were also confident and quick in their mind-blanking reports, with confidence ratings and report latencies matching other off-task thought categories. Subjects didn’t use mind-blanking reports to reflect uncertainty. Study 3 (N = 415) extended our construct-validity investigation to the phenomenology of mind-blanking by separating (within subjects) “mind-blanking” response options into “unclear or foggy thoughts” versus “complete absence of experience.” Unclear thoughts accounted for 3% of thought reports, versus 1% reflecting no experience, suggesting that “blanking” more often reflects diffuse than absent subjective states.

articles_hidden.title: Chronic Pain as a Complex Dynamic System: Conceptual Foundations and a Narrative Review of Network Approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Saskia Scholten; Gwen van der Wijk; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Felicitas Kininger; Julia Glombiewski; Johan W.S. Vlaeyen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Despite extensive medical, psychological, and social research and substantial healthcare investment, chronic pain remains highly prevalent, and a leading cause of years lived with disability. While multimodal and interdisciplinary treatments are recommended, progress may be limited by the lack of an integrative theoretical framework that captures the complexity of chronic pain across levels of analysis.
We introduce a complex dynamic systems perspective as a unifying theoretical framework in which chronic pain emerges from interactions among biological, psychological, and social components over time, and we present a methodological toolbox based on the network approach to operationalize this perspective by modeling such interactions.
We conducted the first narrative review of network studies in chronic pain, identifying 54 studies published up to June 30, 2026. Most studies used cross-sectional network models to examine associations among pain-related variables, comorbidity patterns, and group differences, whereas longitudinal and within-person approaches were rare. Across studies, findings support the view that chronic pain-related factors form interconnected systems; however, substantial heterogeneity in variable selection and study design limits comparability and generalizability.
Overall, current applications provide an important first step toward modeling the complexity of chronic pain but so far remain limited in capturing temporal dynamics and individual-level processes. Advancing this field will require theory-driven, multi-level, and longitudinal research that aligns network methods with system-level questions. In the longer term, this approach holds the promise to support the development of parsimonious models of key mechanisms, informing interventions that target not only symptoms but the dynamic processes that sustain chronic pain.

articles_hidden.title: Does Acquiescence Bias Distort Measurement Invariance Across Multiple Groups? A Monte Carlo Comparison of Tree-Based Factor Analytic Methods
articles_hidden.authors: Tugay Kaçak; David Navarro González
articles_hidden.abstract: Acquiescence (ACQ), the tendency to agree regardless of item content, can differ across groups and thereby mimic or mask measurement non-invariance. Model-based recursive partitioning (MOB) combined with factor-analytic models (e.g. EFAtree, CFAtree) is increasingly used to detect non-invariance across many covariates, but whether the detected heterogeneity can be attributed to its correct source is unknown. In a Monte Carlo simulation (432 conditions, 500 replications each), we compared EFAtree and CFAtree with their random-intercept (RI) versions under four data-generating conditions: groups differed in neither source, in ACQ only, in the content loadings only, or in both. We also propose a block-wise efficient score test that separates instability in the RI variance from instability in the content loadings by projecting out all other parameters. All trees held the nominal Type I error rate. When groups differed only in ACQ, trees without an RI factor mistook the difference for metric non-invariance under unbalanced keying or missed it under balanced keying, whereas the RI trees detected it regardless of keying. Applied to the true grouping variable, the standard block test, which selects a block from the fully decorrelated scores, attributed purely substantive non-invariance to ACQ in 79% of replications, more often in larger samples. The efficient test kept this misattribution near the nominal level (.06) and attributed heterogeneity correctly at the attainable maximum. With one content factor, EFA- and CFA-based trees produced identical results. In an empirical example with the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (N = 26236), the RI variance differed across countries but not across age groups or genders, and even across countries it was only one of several unstable parameter blocks, alongside the intercepts and the factor-mean and factor-variance directions. Before a split is interpreted as measurement non-invariance, its source should be examined with an RI factor and efficient block-wise tests.

articles_hidden.title: A Cluster Randomised Controlled Trial of a Transdiagnostic Preventative Mental Health Intervention for Adolescents: Building Resilience through Socioemotional Training (ReSET)
articles_hidden.authors: Pasco Fearon; Alex Lloyd; Peter Martin; Roslyn Law; Laura Lucas; Tom Chin-Han Wu; Nick Midgley; Nikolaus Steinbeis; René Veenstra; Jaime Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background: Rates of mental health problems in adolescents have increased in the last decade, prompting urgent calls for effective, scalable preventative interventions. To determine whether a novel, group-based, transdiagnostic indicated prevention programme (Building Resilience through Socioemotional Training; ReSET), delivered through existing school mental health provision, improves mental health and wellbeing in at-risk adolescents.
Methods: Two-arm cluster randomised controlled superiority trial (1:1) evaluating ReSET plus usual care versus usual care only, with outcomes assessed immediately post-intervention and at 12-month follow-up. Adolescents aged 12–14 identified through whole-school screening as scoring in the top 25th percentile for overall psychopathology symptoms, in schools selected to over-represent high-need communities (≥30% free school meals eligibility). ReSET is an 8-session group -based intervention that targets two key mechanisms implicated in risk for psychopathology in adolescents – social functioning and emotional processing. Pre-registered co-primary outcomes were overall self-reported psychopathology (SDQ) and wellbeing (WEMWBS), assessed immediately post-intervention and at 12-month follow-up.
Results: Of 4,005 adolescents screened, 1465 met eligibility, 727 consented and 560 were enrolled. There was no evidence of intervention effects on either co-primary outcome immediately post-intervention. At 12-month follow-up, there was evidence of improvement in overall psychopathology (adjusted mean difference −1.36, 97.5% CI −2.23 to −0.50, p=0.0004; SMD=0.25, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.42). Secondary outcomes showed a consistent pattern: no effects immediately post-intervention, but significant benefits for anxiety, depression, general psychopathology, and internalising symptoms at 12-month follow-up. No effects on externalising symptoms were observed at either timepoint.
Conclusions: The delayed emergence of benefit is consistent with a skills-based prevention model in which adolescents acquire skills that support resilient functioning when facing subsequent emotional and interpersonal challenges. These findings suggest that transdiagnostic interventions targeting socioemotional processes have the potential to prevent common adolescent mental health problems, though replication and longer-term evaluation are needed.

articles_hidden.title: Inter-trial intervals bias reinforcement learning in humans
articles_hidden.authors: Noa Yadid; Omer Linkovski; Paul B. Sharp
articles_hidden.abstract: Although we know humans attempt to maximize reward per unit time when foraging, it remains unclear how the common practice of varying waiting time via inter-trial intervals (ITI) impacts reinforcement learning. Here, we tested several hypotheses concerning how time to wait during the ITI impacts reinforcement learning, including replay of recent outcomes, sensory decay of action representations, and discounting of action values due to added time costs. To test which of these accounts explains how ITIs impact reinforcement learning, we conducted a series of bandit-style tasks in which the ITI was either 1 or 4 seconds, expecting longer ITIs to allow replay that strengthens recent learning. Instead, across four studies (n = 96, 96, 439 and 117), a longer ITI made people more likely to change their last choice selectively after wins but not after losses. To explain why this effect occurs, we used computational modeling to demonstrate how the ITI cost competes with learned value for control of the next choice, with time costs impacting choice more when learned values were more uncertain. The effect of ITIs on choice generalized to a public fMRI dataset with jittered ITIs, and was absent in language-model agents playing our task. Taken together, our results suggest that ITIs bias human reinforcement learning, where people try to reduce uncontrollable time costs through switching to a new choice.

articles_hidden.title: Low-Vision Navigation Reveals Shortcomings of Current Navigation Frameworks: Proposals for Experiments and Design
articles_hidden.authors: Jack Morris; Bastien Perroy; Roberto Casati
articles_hidden.abstract: People with low vision (PLVs) experience difficulties in spatial navigation associated with their low vision (LV) and are inadequately supported by status quo information solutions. The LV case, in which visual input is present but functionally unreliable, also falls out of scope of existing taxonomies of spatial navigation derived from mostly normally sighted subjects. We propose three perturbations through which LV adds attentional demands to navigation: we review evidence that it de-automates the task of avoiding obstacles and safely walking (vigilant locomotion), hypothesize that it strains visual search by creating uncertainty about information sources’ presence, placement, form, and accessibility (naive search), and conjecture that it lowers confidence for wayfinding decisions, encouraging backtracking and frequent confirmation (fragile decisions). Empirical evidence supports that vigilant locomotion under LV interferes with concurrent cognitive processes, especially spatial learning. We hypothesize that this interference extends to wayfinding and that difficulties in information sampling (naive search) and low metacognitive confidence (fragile decisions) additionally strain attention. Accordingly, we introduce three design aims which can help evaluate whether current and prospective wayfinding information solutions support low-vision navigation by addressing these perturbations; information should be continuous at step-level, easy to sample, and confirmatory via paired feedback. Future research should directly test these predictions in ecological contexts and investigate the possibility that acute stressors can mimic the LV-related perturbations in the general population.

articles_hidden.title: Experiment-based calibration in psychology: foundational and data-generating model
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik R Bach
articles_hidden.abstract:
Experiment-based calibration is a novel method for measurement validation, which – unlike classical validity metrics – does not require stable between-person variance. In this approach, the latent variable to be measured
is manipulated by an experiment, and its predicted scores – termed standard scores – are compared against the measured scores. Previous work has shown that under plausible boundary conditions, the correlation
between standard and measured scores – termed retrodictive validity – is informative about measurement accuracy, i.e. combined trueness and precision. Here, I expand these findings in several directions. First, I
formalise the approach in a probability-theoretic framework with the concept of a standardised calibration space. Second, I relate this framework to classical validity theory and show that the boundary conditions
in fact apply to any form of criterion validity, including classical convergent validity. Thus, I state precise and empirically quantifiable boundary conditions under which criterion validity metrics are informative on
validity. Third, I relate these boundary conditions to confounding variables, i.e. correlated latent variables. I show that in the limit, calibration will converge on the latent variable that is most closely related to the
standard. Finally, I provide a framework for modelling the data-generating process with Markov kernels, and identify sufficient conditions under which the data generation model results in a calibration space. In sum,
this article provides a formal probability-theoretic framework for experiment-based calibration and facilitates modelling and empirical assessment of the data generating processes.

articles_hidden.title: Virtual Reality Simulation of Prosthesis embodiment: A Multimodal Investigation Examining Gaze Behaviour and Sense of agency
articles_hidden.authors: David Crevillén Hernández; Bigna Lenggenhager; Cosimo Gentile; Laura Zapparoli; Roberto Meattini; Gianluca Saetta; Emily S. Cross
articles_hidden.abstract: Suffering a limb amputation has a major impact on physical and psychological health, with prosthetic devices being a fundamental tool to mitigate it. Prosthesis embodiment (integrating a prosthetic device into the bodily self) is a fundamental process for accepting these devices, with the sense of agency (the experience of controlling one’s actions and, through them, the course of external events) as a key contributing factor. Current upper-limb myoelectric prostheses still present high abandonment rates, partly due to motor-control errors that may reduce the sense of agency associated with prosthesis movements. One possible solution is sharing motor autonomy between the user and a grasping intention-detection algorithm, with prosthetic movements combining user actions and inferred intentions. In this study, we investigated whether shared autonomy, simulated through automated grasp assistance by an idealised intention-detection system in immersive virtual reality, influences explicit (self-reported) and implicit (indirectly assessed) sense of agency, prosthesis embodiment, task performance, and gaze behaviour. Fifty-seven able-bodied participants completed an object repositioning task over an obstacle with prosthetic avatars that varied in motor autonomy and appearance. Shared autonomy increased self-reported agency and reduced failed attempts. However, neither appearance nor motor autonomy affected embodiment scores. Although explicit and implicit measures of agency were significantly correlated, they responded differently to experimental manipulations. Shared autonomy increased explicit but not implicit agency, while longer action–outcome delays were associated with reduced explicit agency but stronger intentional binding.  revealing dissociations across conditions and action-outcome delays. Additionally, explicit agency was associated with reduced visual attention towards the prosthesis and manipulated object. Together, these results indicate that shared autonomy approaches can enhance control experience and improve task performance while highlighting distinctions between explicit and implicit agency measures during prosthesis control.

articles_hidden.title: When Effort Invigorates:  Instrumental Effort History Increases Cue-Evoked Response Vigour While Preserving Outcome-Specific Transfer
articles_hidden.authors: Yulong Huang; Zhang Chen; Ruth Krebs; Lara Bardi
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental cues can influence action through outcome-related information learned elsewhere, but whether features of the instrumental acquisition history associated with those outcomes remain behaviourally relevant when the outcomes are later predicted by Pavlovian cues is unknown. Across two experiments, one conducted in the laboratory (N = 54) and one online (N = 67), we separated instrumental acquisition under low- and high-effort response requirements from Pavlovian cue learning. Participants first learned that different actions produced outcomes under relatively low or high effort requirements and separately learned cues predicting those same outcomes. Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer (PIT) was then tested under extinction, with neither outcomes nor response requirements present. In both experiments, reward-predictive cues elicited greater response vigour than a control cue. Critically, cues predicting outcomes previously obtained under high-effort response requirements elicited greater responding than cues predicting outcomes obtained under low-effort requirements. Specific PIT was robust under both acquisition conditions, with cues selectively promoting actions associated with their predicted outcomes. There was also suggestive evidence that high-effort acquisition amplified the magnitude of specific PIT, but this modulation was not consistently supported across experiments or statistical approaches. No corresponding effect emerged for initial outcome-congruent action selection. Overall, response vigour was modulated by instrumental effort history more consistently than outcome-specific action selection, indicating that features of prior effortful instrumental experience can remain behaviourally relevant when the associated outcomes are later predicted by separately learned Pavlovian cues.

articles_hidden.title: The relationship between deictic relating and theory of mind
articles_hidden.authors: Maura Nevejans; Jamie Cummins; Jan De Houwer; Emiel Cracco; Yulong Huang; Jan R. Wiersema
articles_hidden.abstract: Relational Frame Theory (RFT) proposes that deictic relating plays a critical role in “Theory of Mind” (ToM). However, empirical research to date on the relationship between deictic relating and ToM has been inconclusive, potentially due to small sample sizes and limitations in the assessment of deictic relating. In the present online study (N = 164), we tested the relationship between deictic relating and two ToM measures: a low-level ToM task (a visual perspective-taking task) and a high-level ToM task (the Faux Pas Recognition Test). We additionally tested associations with general cognitive ability and autism traits. Based on predictions from RFT, we hypothesized that deictic relating would correlate with both ToM measures, with a stronger association for low-level ToM. We observed a positive correlation of deictic relating with performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, whereas its correlation with visual perspective-taking was non-significant for our primary outcome measure. Opposite to predictions derived from RFT, deictic relating was positively correlated with autism traits, whereas scores on the Faux Pas Recognition Test and visual perspective-taking task were not significantly correlated with autism traits. Although these findings may suggest a relationship between deictic relating and ToM, the absence of an association with low-level ToM is difficult to reconcile with RFT. Alternative explanations for observed correlations, including task characteristics or other related abilities, are discussed. Finally, the finding that higher scores on the autism traits questionnaire were related to better deictic relating is at odds with RFT and raises questions about which abilities the task measures.

articles_hidden.title: Development and validation of a task for assessing help-seeker relational dynamics.
articles_hidden.authors: Tyler Kwan; Orestis Zavlis; Caroline Selai; Michael Moutoussis
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-other evaluations play a crucial role in understanding psychiatric disorders and improving collaboration between service users and providers. However, experimental paradigms of such relational processes tend to have low reliability and ecological validity. Quantitative analyses can validate the task’s measurement properties while qualitative analyses can empower service users to provide novel insights about task development and interpretation. In this study, we use both quantitative and qualitative analyses to develop the “Helping Task” based on the iterated prisoner’s dilemma. In this task, help-seeking participants knowingly engaged in an asymmetric relationship with a computerized help-provider, in which both parties invested effort (points). Initial qualitative feedback from 17 individuals (15 ‘neurotypical’, 2 having lived experience of relational difficulties) was used to refine key task properties (like task instructions, interface labels, and general navigation). Subsequent thematic analyses revealed that these participants interpreted helping exchanges through expectations about reciprocity, moral obligations, and underlying mental intentions, mirroring descriptions of real helping relationships. Moreover, quantitative analyses of 30 online participants validated the task’s sensitivity to helper behaviour and the within-session reliability of mean trust, decision satisfaction, and intended effort. Finally, computational analyses revealed probabilistic states in which trust, decision satisfaction, and effort were jointly lower or higher, indicating that self-other evaluations were linked to willingness to invest in the relationship. These findings support the reliability and validity of the Helping Task and pave the way for computational studies of self-other evaluations in helping relationships.

articles_hidden.title: Electrophysiological correlates underlying the use of generated affective music to regulate stress in individuals with elevated anxiety
articles_hidden.authors: Gladys Jiamin Heng; Claudia Kahrs; Lily T. Smith; Stefan K. Ehrlich; Cuntai Guan; Kat Agres
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent advances in generative music systems offer new opportunities for supporting stress regulation in individuals experiencing psychological distress. However, the degree to which music should reflect the desired relaxation state, and the neural dynamics underlying music-based regulation, are not well understood. The present study investigated the electrophysiological correlates of stress reduction using generated music that expresses different degrees of relaxation. Twenty-seven adults (10M, age: 31.33 ± 9.65 years) with elevated anxiety (measured by the Depression, Anxiety, Stress Scale-21) completed three blocks of a stress-inducing arithmetic task, each followed by three minutes of silence, Low-relaxation music (Low-RM), or High-relaxation music (High-RM). Low-RM anchored musical characteristics near participants’ post-stress affect ratings; High-RM shifted these parameters 30% toward positive-valence and low-arousal. Following stress induction, subjective valence increased in both music conditions but arousal decreased only in High-RM and silence. Relative to silence, frontal delta suppression was observed in both music conditions, with additional parietal delta suppression in Low-RM. Exploratory analyses identified parieto-occipital alpha suppression during High-RM. Across conditions, greater frontal delta reduction was associated with lower Anxiety scores. These findings provide new insights for the efficacy of affective generated music in modulating neurophysiological processes implicated in stress regulation for individuals with elevated anxiety.

articles_hidden.title: Overestimated Volatility Underpins Aberrant Decision Making in Bipolar I Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Juha Lee; Jinwoo Jeong; Jerome R Busemeyer; Brian F. O'Donnell; Woo-Young Ahn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background 
Bipolar disorder (BD) is marked by extreme mood fluctuations, yet the computational mechanisms underlying this instability remain poorly understood. Recent computational accounts suggest that mood instability may arise from altered reward prediction error (RPE) processing, yet little is known about the factors that modulate this process. Volatility inference—the ability to track environmental change—may be particularly relevant as it modulates the influence of prediction errors on belief updating. However, it remains unclear whether BD is characterized by altered volatility inference.
Method 
We investigated whether BD showed altered volatility inference across distinct environmental structures using decision-making tasks and computational modeling. Individuals with bipolar I disorder (BD-I; N = 32) and healthy controls (HC; N = 40) completed two tasks: a probability-tracking task (PTT) with predetermined contingency changes across stable and volatile phases and a probabilistic reversal learning task (PRL) with performance-contingent reversals.
Results 
The BD-I group showed reduced performance and switched choices more frequently than the HC group across both tasks. Computational modeling further revealed heightened volatility beliefs in the BD-I group, reflected by a higher prior belief about volatility in the PTT and higher tonic volatility in the PRL, together with greater behavioral stochasticity across both tasks. These computational alterations were not associated with current manic or depressive symptom severity.
Conclusions 
These findings suggest that BD-I shows deficits in adapting to volatile environments, potentially arising from trait-like computational alterations characterized by heightened expectations of environmental change and noisy belief-to-action mapping, which may provide candidate mechanisms through which decision-making abnormalities contribute to mood instability.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of the Short UPPS-P Impulsive Behavior Scale in Danish adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Genevieve Fullerton Dash; Alex P. Miller; Emese Kroon; Lotte Valentin-Holbech; Sarah W. Feldstein Ewing; Kristine Rømer Thomsen
articles_hidden.abstract: Purpose. The short UPPS-P (SUPPS-P) is a widely used, gold-standard measure capturing five facets of impulsivity, including negative urgency, (lack of) premeditation, (lack of) perseverance, sensation seeking, and positive urgency. However, most validation studies have been conducted in relatively small convenience samples, few utilize multi-wave data, and no formal psychometric evaluation of the SUPPS-P has been conducted in a Danish sample. Procedures. Up to 2,745 adolescents (65.46% female, Mage=16.77 [SD=0.58] at baseline) completed the Danish SUPPS-P, as well as measures of substance use, self-efficacy, well-being, and internalizing symptoms at four timepoints over a 12-month period. Confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to evaluate fit of the established SUPPS-P five-factor structure and test measurement invariance across biological sex. Convergent, discriminant, and predictive validity; internal consistency; and test-retest reliability were evaluated for each subscale. Main Findings. Replicating past studies, a five-factor model best fit the data, but several items loaded weakly on the lack of perseverance and sensation seeking factors. Measurement invariance across biological sex was established. Positive correlations with substance use, negative correlations with self-efficacy and well-being, and subscale-specific correlations with internalizing symptoms supported convergent and discriminant validity. Correlations of baseline SUPPS-P scores with external variables up to 12 months later supported predictive validity. Internal consistency was acceptable for all subscales (ω=0.67-0.81) and moderate intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC=0.51-0.69) supported adequate test-retest reliability. Conclusions. The SUPPS-P is suitable for assessing impulsivity in Danish adolescents over time, though further research is needed to optimize the measure’s psychometric properties in this group.

articles_hidden.title: Memory strength drives hybrid search efficiency
articles_hidden.authors: Dyllan Simpson; Lauren Williams; Haven Vander Bie; Viola S. Störmer; Timothy F. Brady
articles_hidden.abstract: In hybrid search tasks, observers search for any of multiple targets held in memory (e.g., finding all of the ingredients for a recipe in the supermarket). Performance declines with the log of the number of memorized targets, a cost often attributed to a serial scan through memory. In standard models of recognition memory, however, holding more items in memory weakens the match strength between each memory representation and the corresponding visual item – independent of any serial search process. Here we propose an account of hybrid search based on memory strength, testing how memory strength affects hybrid search separately from memory set size. We found that strengthening memories through repetition and deeper encoding improved hybrid search at matched set sizes (Exp. 1). Taking advantage of NFL and NHL fans' pre-existing memory strength for sports logos (Exps. 2–3), we next found search was better for a larger set of familiar items (16 logos) than for a smaller set of unfamiliar items (12 logos), a reversal of the usual memory set-size effect. A standard global matching model (REM), with encoding parameters fit only to memory performance, not search data, reproduced these results and the canonical, approximately log-linear set-size cost in discriminability. Memory strength is thus a potentially strong determinant of hybrid search efficiency, with set-size effects not necessarily reflecting any serial memory search. Instead, models of recognition memory may provide a productive framework for the memory component of hybrid search.

articles_hidden.title: Coupled social dilemmas reveal positive cross-game transfer in humans and contrasting cue use in tested GPT agents
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Salahshour; Sumanth Bhargava; Tim Johnson; Iain Couzin
articles_hidden.abstract: Cooperation across social settings requires deciding whether to reciprocate a partner’s helpful behavior or exploit it when incentives change. We examined this tension in an online experiment with 430 participants playing a Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD), either alone or followed by a Snowdrift game (SD), where defection pays more against a sufficiently likely cooperator. We also placed programmed bots—computer-controlled players following a fixed rule—in some groups. By programming them to cooperate in PD and reciprocate their partner’s PD action in SD, we created a consistent source of cooperation and reciprocity. This allowed us to ask whether humans also cooperated more with one another. Humans cooperated more in SD after their partner cooperated in PD, even when observed partner behavior made defection the better immediate material response. This pattern is consistent with reciprocity, although choices do not identify beliefs or motives. Human–human cooperation was higher in groups containing bots; coupling alone produced no detected increase in mean PD cooperation. Separate experiments with GPT language-model agents asked whether frequent cooperation was accompanied by similar responses across games. Despite high PD cooperation, partner PD cooperation predicted less GPT cooperation in SD in the primary pooled analysis. This association varied across configurations and did not generally indicate payoff-maximizing choices. Simulations using fitted human response rules illustrated the possible effects of alternative bot policies. These findings reveal responses to cooperative partners across contexts that overall cooperation rates can obscure.

articles_hidden.title: User Engagement Strategies for Digital Medication Adherence Interventions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Serena Thaw-Poon; Isabella Diaz; Candice Acevedo; Tanisa Goyal; Dayanara Salinas; Jannine Balakid; Cyd Eaton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Medication adherence is critical for chronic disease management, yet poor adherence remains an unsolved challenge. Digital health interventions are promising to support medication adherence but are limited by poor user engagement with the tools. Understanding which strategies effectively support user engagement could improve the efficacy and sustainability of these interventions.
Purpose: This systematic review and meta-analysis characterized strategies used to support user engagement in digital adherence interventions with the well-established Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy and evaluated whether these strategies were associated with medication adherence and user engagement outcomes. 
Methods: Electronic databases (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), Embase via Ovid, MEDLINE, PsycInfo, and Web of Science Core Collection) were searched (4/18/2025) to identify randomized controlled trials of app-based digital adherence interventions for people with chronic medical conditions taking oral medications, published in English between 2020 and 2025. User engagement strategies were characterized with the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy. Meta-regression models evaluated associations between specific techniques and study outcomes. Risk of bias was characterized with the Risk of Bias-1 measure.  
Results: The 60 studies included for review predominantly included adults with cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes (median N=117, IQR=72.0-204.5). All but one included at least one user engagement strategy appropriate to characterize with the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy. The most common techniques were Prompts/cues (90%), Instruction on how to perform the behavior (70%), Adding objects to the environment (35%), Feedback on behavior (28%), Self-monitoring of behavior (25%), Credible source (22%), Goal setting (behavior) (20%), and Self-monitoring outcome(s) of behavior (20%). Prompts/cues were frequently paired with another behavior change technique (54%). User engagement was rarely measured as an outcome, and thus, it was not possible to evaluate this outcome in the meta-analysis. In the 44 studies included in the meta-analysis of medication adherence outcomes, there were no statistically significant associations with user engagement techniques.  
Conclusions: Digital adherence interventions commonly include strategies to support user engagement, particularly prompts/cues, but it remains unknown whether these strategies translate to actual user engagement. No user engagement strategy was associated with medication adherence outcomes. This may reflect variability across study samples and medication adherence measurement approaches, threats to internal validity, or reliance on ineffective strategies. Further research should continue to evaluate which engagement strategies support sustained digital adherence tool use and improved adherence outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Informing WHO Guidance on Learning Health Systems for the Implementation, Scale-Up and Sustainment of Evidence-Informed Health Interventions: Findings from an  International Stakeholder Consultation
articles_hidden.authors: Rachel Sutherland; Anna Rayward; Sam McCrabb; Heidi Turon; Cassandra Lane; Courtney Barnes; Lucy Couper; Nicole Nathan; Vanessa Rose; Davi Mamblona Marques Romão
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Learning Health Systems (LHSs) have considerable potential to improve the implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-informed health interventions. 
However, practical guidance on operationalising LHS principles across diverse health system contexts, levels (macro, meso, and micro), and stakeholder groups remains 
limited. To support broader adoption, the World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with the University of Newcastle's National Centre of Implementation 
Science (NCOIS), developed a draft Guidance on using a Learning Health System approach to implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-informed health 
interventions (Guidance). An international stakeholder consultation was undertaken to inform its refinement.
Objectives
The consultation sought feedback to: (1) assess the relevance and applicability of the draft Guidance; (2) identify implementation considerations across diverse settings; and (3) 
obtain recommendations to improve its content, usability, and practical application.
Process
Stakeholders from policymaking, research, clinical, and other health system sectors 
2
across all six WHO regions were invited by the WHO Evidence-Informed Policy Network 
(EVIPNet) to attend a two-hour online workshop conducted in April 2025 via Zoom. 
Participants received background materials in advance. Facilitated breakout discussions focused on: (1) content and structure; and (2) dissemination, implementation, and 
practical application. Feedback was collected from multiple sources (e.g., discussion notes, Zoom chats) and synthesised by NCOIS staff involved in the Guidance
development.
Key Messages and Feedback Impact
Participants expressed strong support for the purpose and value of the Guidance. Feedback emphasised the need for flexible, iterative approaches that accommodate 
variation in health system contexts, levels, stakeholder needs, and available resources. Participants highlighted the importance of supporting progressive development of LHS 
capabilities and strongly endorsed accessible language, case studies, practical tools, and alignment with existing WHO frameworks.
Feedback informed refinements to improve clarity, accessibility, and practical applicability. Revisions strengthened content on LHS concepts, implementation, leadership and governance, stakeholder engagement, and equity, while adding case studies, implementation tools, resource inventories, and practical supports.
Conclusion
The consultation provided a robust mechanism to assess and strengthen the relevance, usability, feasibility, and acceptability of the Guidance. The resulting refinements enhanced its applicability across diverse settings and its potential to support implementation, scale-up and sustainment using an LHS approach.

articles_hidden.title: Publications in Psychiatry: Modern Historical Trends and Sociodemographic Factors (2000-2022)
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Cavallaro; Alessandro Carollo; Marc H. Bornstein; Gianluca Esposito
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and objectives: Psychiatric research has grown significantly in recent years, with an increase in scientific publications worldwide. However, the factors associated with these trends remain insufficiently explored. This study examines the country-level correlates of psychiatric research output across countries, focusing on economic, demographic, and development-related variables. The analysis considers the annual number of publications, Gross Domestic Product (GDP), population size and density, and the Human Development Index (HDI). Methods: Data were retrieved from Web of Science and considered all publications categorized under "Psychiatry" from 2000 to 2022. The study period was selected to ensure consistency with demographic and economic datasets, for which data were available through 2022. Generalized linear mixed model were employed to estimate the associations of GDP, population, and HDI with publication output. Results: At the global level, GDP and HDI showed significant positive associations with both absolute and relative psychiatric publication frequency (ps < .001). Population size was positively associated with absolute frequency but negatively associated with relative frequency, whereas population density was positively associated only with absolute frequency. In the continent-specific analyses, HDI was positively associated with both outcomes in all six continents. Exploratory analyses of its components revealed greater regional differentiation: education-related indicators showed the most consistent positive associations, whereas gross national income per capita and life expectancy varied across continents in their direction and statistical significance. Conclusion: This study provides a comprehensive overview of global trends in psychiatric research and their most associated factors. The results underscore the importance of economic growth and
human development in fostering scientific productivity, with substantial variation across continents.

articles_hidden.title: Emerging Insights into Cognitive Control from Computational Models of Choice
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Samuel Weigard; Andrew Heathcote; Chandra Sripada
articles_hidden.abstract: Research into cognitive control has flourished over the last three decades across many areas of the psychological and neural sciences, but problems have recently emerged that raise foundational questions about what cognitive control is, how individual differences should be measured, and the validity of cognitive control as an explanation for variation in behavioral traits and clinical conditions. Here, we outline a novel perspective that is rooted in evidence accumulation models, formal mathematical models that explain how individuals make choices across many contexts. We review model-based work that distinguishes conflict-specific processes, which are selectively engaged to address goal-conflicting information, from task-general processes that facilitate goal-relevant responding irrespective of the presence of conflict. This review reveals an emerging consensus that task-general, but not conflict-specific, processes show validity as coherent individual difference dimensions. We then highlight the computationally-derived measure we call efficiency of evidence accumulation (EEA) that reflects the amplification of goal-relevant information across many tasks and contexts. EEA shows strong validity as a trait-like individual difference dimension, explains individual differences in performance in cognitive control tasks, and shows clear relevance to behavioral traits and clinical conditions in which cognitive control, as traditionally defined, is thought to be impaired. These findings help address multiple theoretical, methodological, and empirical challenges in the study of control processes in cognition, indicate that characterizing processes that enhance goal-relevant responding across contexts is a promising way forward, and suggest important ways in which theories of control’s role in behavioral outcomes could be revised.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-informed Psychoeducation for Anorexia Nervosa: From Genetics to Neuroplasticity
articles_hidden.authors: Kara Kerr; Danielle DeVille
articles_hidden.abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a debilitating and often chronic disorder associated with significant morbidity and mortality. In recent decades, research on AN has identified key neurobiological pathways and brain regions that likely contribute to risk for and maintenance of the disorder and its symptoms. These include alterations in neurocircuitry underlying fear, motivation and reward, interoception, habit formation, and cognitive control, in addition to the detrimental effects of malnutrition on brain structure and function. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) for AN can be integrated with existing therapeutic approaches to improve patients’ and families’ understanding of the disorder and engagement in treatment. This chapter outlines content, strategies, and considerations for the effective implementation of NIPE in the treatment of AN.

articles_hidden.title: The Illusion of Routine Knowledge:  Time-Specific Expectations Weakly Predict Behavior on Sampled Occasions
articles_hidden.authors: Stephanie Aurora Cárdenas; Rosalba Linares
articles_hidden.abstract: People report as memories not only what they retrieve, but what seems plausible. Routine knowledge may inform plausibility judgments and support accurate reconstruction when behavior follows an expected routine. But how often does behavior match those routine expectations? We conducted preregistered analyses of previously collected longitudinal data from student and community samples (N = 207; Cárdenas et al., 2021). We compared expected routines for 18,736 day-and-hour periods—e.g., Tuesdays, 1-2 PM—with 3,510 one-time experience-sampled occasions and 725 retrospective reports. Participants expected complete routines during 92.83% of waking-hour periods, but behavior matched at least two of three expected domains on only 44.39% of occasions expected to be highly typical. Expected typicality did not reliably predict recall accuracy. Exploratorily, higher expected typicality predicted greater schema reliance: retrospective reports reproduced expectations that had not matched sampled behavior. Routine knowledge may provide a less reliable basis for reconstruction than participants’ confidence in their routines suggests.

articles_hidden.title: Color preferences in dogs: A replication study
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey R Stevens; Anwyn Gatesy-Davis; Susannah Couture; Yasmin Worth
articles_hidden.abstract: Free-ranging dogs (Canis familiaris) in India have been shown to prefer approaching yellow bowls before blue and grey ones (Roy et al. (2025). Animal Cognition, 28(1), 1–9). However, it is not clear if this preference for the color yellow is specific to free-ranging dogs in India or whether it generalizes to other dog populations. We conducted a replication of the Roy et al. study to assess whether pet dogs in the United States show similar preferences by measuring whether they approached yellow, blue, or grey bowls first. We conducted two experiments and found that pet dogs younger than seven years old first approached yellow bowls most often, replicating Roy et al.'s findings. To test if brightness rather than color accounted for this preference, we conducted a third preference experiment with light, medium, and dark grey bowls. The dogs did not prefer the light grey bowl, indicating that there was not a preference for the brightest achromatic stimulus. Therefore, a preference for yellow food-related objects extends beyond free-ranging dogs to our sample of pet dogs. Understanding dog color preferences is important for guiding the design of dog products and environments but also is critical for canine behavioral scientists who must make decisions about colors for experimental stimuli.

articles_hidden.title: Do thoughts actually drive symptoms? Testing cognitive theories of posttraumatic stress with natural language processing in daily diaries
articles_hidden.authors: Whitney R. Ringwald; Vasudha Varadarajan; Scott Feltman; H. Andrew Schwartz; Adithya V Ganesan; Oscar Nils Erik Kjell; Michael Zvolensky; Benjamin Luft; Roman Kotov
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive theories are among the leading conceptualizations of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).  The core perspective shared by these theories is that distorted thinking (e.g., “no one can be trusted”) is involved in maintaining symptoms.  However, the proximal mechanisms linking cognition and PTSD symptoms remains unclear due to two major methodological limitations: 1) lack of research on cognition-symptom dynamics at the daily level, and 2) reliance on self-reported thought distortions, which is a method ill-suited for capturing biases that people often do not have insight into or are outside of their awareness. The present study helps address these limitations in a sample of trauma-exposed patients (N=510) who completed daily video diaries and symptom ratings for 90 days (n=30,958 days).  We used two natural language processing techniques to assess cognitive distortions from the diary transcripts: a lexica-based and large language model (LLM) approach. We then established the day-to-day sequencing of cognitive distortion and symptom fluctuations using dynamic structural equation models.  Across the lexical and LLM models, distorted thinking did not predict worsening symptoms (bs=-.02–.01).  Instead, worsening symptoms predicted more distorted thinking (bs=.03–.07). Also, symptoms and cognitive distortions tended to fluctuate together (bs=.08–.41). The current findings suggest that cognitive distortions do not precede PTSD symptoms as many theories have assumed, but may instead be a consequence or correlate of them. If replicated, our results could help refine cognitive and related models of PTSD.

articles_hidden.title: Consensus-based TRansparent, sUStainable, and Transferable (TRUST) best-practice guidelines for visual word recognition research
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Gagl; Xenia Schmalz; Karo Brimmers; Sascha Schroeder; Jascha Rüsseler; Fritz Günther; Monika Tschense; Silvia Brem; Marc Brysbaert; Hanna Woloszyn
articles_hidden.abstract: Reading is a fundamental life skill, and at its basis is the ability to process single words. Researchers often study single-word processing using lexical decision tasks. However, most research is conducted in a single language by separate research groups, limiting comparability, replicability, and generalizability. In addition, best-practice knowledge is often only transmitted informally within labs, leading to heterogeneity and reduced reproducibility across labs. Here, we, the TRUST Consortium, established a consensus-based research guideline for current best practices in psycholinguistic reading research by integrating expert knowledge. We used German as a case study and formulated guidelines for visual lexical decision experiments. We reached consortium-level consensus through multiple feedback circles and quantified agreement using importance ratings. The guidelines are openly available as a living guideline document on a webpage (trust-guidelines-v01.readthedocs.io), with git-versioning infrastructure that makes changes transparent and enables discussion. To validate the guidelines, we implemented the German Lexicon Project, providing an empirical feedback loop to test our suggestions. The living, open nature of the guidelines invites broader community feedback. It also enables future extension to other languages, groups (e.g., dyslexics), and methods (e.g., brain imaging), as it is openly available and includes instructions for hosting an adapted version at no cost. Thus, we provide a document intended to raise research standards in reading research worldwide, as a service to the community, potentially increasing replication rates and generalizability of relevant effects and phenomena.

articles_hidden.title: The impact of meditation on cognitive flexibility: A critical review and the case for investigating True Self Meditation
articles_hidden.authors: Cecilia Jimyung Nam; Boas Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive flexibility, the capacity to adapt thinking and behavior in response to changing environmental demands, is a critical component of psychological resilience and executive functioning. Meditation, particularly attention-based practices, has been associated with improvements in core cognitive processes, such as sustained attention, emotion regulation, and metacognitive awareness. Neuroimaging and behavioral evidence suggests that meditation activates neural networks involving the prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and limbic regions, which are crucial for set-shifting, adaptive learning, and executive control. While much of the current literature centers on Mindfulness Meditation, this focus has primarily served as a foundational framework for understanding meditation's cognitive effects. Other meditation modalities remain comparatively less explored in scientific literature, particularly in Western academic contexts. True Self Meditation (TSM), a practice rooted in systematic emotional and cognitive reflection, represents a compelling but under-recognized area for investigation. TSM involves the active identification and systematic discarding of maladaptive emotional images, promoting positive, resilient cognitive patterns. Existing research suggests that TSM may directly target cognitive flexibility mechanisms by engaging neural processes related to memory storage, emotional regulation, and executive functioning. Moreover, TSM-based interventions have demonstrated significant improvements in psychological well-being, social adjustment, and neurocognitive activation. While a substantial body of self-report and observational research-particularly within South Korea-has examined TSM's psychological outcomes, limited work has investigated its neurocognitive mechanisms or broader applicability across diverse populations. This review synthesizes existing research on TSM's potential impact on cognitive flexibility , focusing on neural mechanisms and methodological strengths and weaknesses in the literature. Addressing these gaps could offer valuable insight into how specific meditation practices differentially influence cognitive functioning. Future research should prioritize experimental, neuroimaging, and longitudinal approaches to clarify TSM's cognitive effects and potential as a targeted intervention. Expanding TSM's research will help capture the diversity of meditative practices and their unique contributions to cognitive and clinical outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Same, same but different: Executive functioning and eating behavior profiles among weight management participants
articles_hidden.authors: Marc Yangüez; Julissa Ruiz; Hollie Raynor; Aaron R. Seitz; Sarah Salvy
articles_hidden.abstract: Executive functions (EF) are associated with weight management, yet the two common ways of measuring them, cognitive tasks and self-report questionnaires of everyday functioning, rarely agree. The present study examined whether combining both types of measures reveals distinct profiles of EF and how these relate to age, body mass index (BMI), and eating behaviors. Methods: Adults enrolled in a behavioral weight-loss intervention (N = 277; 84% women; mean BMI 33.9 kg/m²) completed diverse cognitive tasks tapping EF, the BRIEF-A, and the Dutch Eating Behavior Questionnaire. Bayesian factor analyses captured task-based (inhibitory control, working memory) and self-reported (behavioral regulation, emotional regulation, metacognition) EF latent factors, which were entered into a latent profile analysis with age, BMI, and restrained, emotional, and external eating. Results: Task-based and self-reported EF factors were essentially uncorrelated. Three profiles emerged (entropy = 0.82): (i) higher EF task performance with few self-reported difficulties, (ii) lower EF task performance with few self-reported difficulties in older participants, and (iii) average EF task performance with more self-reported difficulties and the highest emotional and external eating. BMI and restrained eating were similar across profiles. Conclusions: Adults with similar BMI had distinct combinations of cognitive performance, everyday executive difficulties, and eating behaviors. Emotional and external eating were linked to self-reported EF difficulties rather than EF task performance, suggesting that self-report EF measures add clinically relevant information. Future work should test whether these profiles predict adherence and weight loss.

articles_hidden.title: Brief Report: Examining Sleep Challenges in Down Syndrome
articles_hidden.authors: Kaylie Burns; Anna Pyle; S. Justin Thomas; Sylvie Mrug; Caroline G. Richter
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Sleep disturbances, common in Down syndrome (DS), adversely affect daily functioning and quality of life across the lifespan. However, little is known about behavioral sleep problems in adolescents and young adults with DS, including age and sex differences, as well as agreement between caregiver- and self-reports of sleep. 
Methods
Study 1 included 24 individuals with DS (37% female, Mage=18.33 years, SD=4.38) and their caregivers, who completed six dichotomous questions assessing bedtime resistance, prolonged sleep onset latency, inappropriate sleep location, nighttime awakenings, early morning awakenings, and daytime sleepiness. After estimating prevalence, binomial logistic regressions tested age and sex differences in each problem. Study 2 included 12 caregiver-participant dyads (25% female, Mage=29.17 years, SD=8.99) who completed parallel self- and caregiver-report forms of the Children's Report of Sleep Patterns (CRSP). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, ICCs and Spearman rank-order correlations examined reporter differences, absolute agreement and associations.
Results
In Study 1, daytime sleepiness was most prevalent (92%), followed by bedtime resistance (79%), nighttime awakenings (75%), prolonged sleep onset latency (58%), early morning awakenings (54%), and inappropriate sleep location (46%). Older age was associated with increased odds of prolonged sleep onset latency; no other age or sex-specific associations were significant. In Study 2, caregiver and self-reports differed significantly for sleep location, bedtime fears, restless legs, insomnia, and enuresis. Associations and absolute agreement were generally limited, although Weekend Bedtime showed the strongest correspondence between reporters.
Conclusions
Sleep problems are highly prevalent in adolescents and young adults with DS, with greater sleep onset difficulties at older ages. Caregiver- and self-reports provide complementary rather than interchangeable information, supporting the need for multi-informant sleep assessment.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Consequences of Challenge: the Degree to which Spoken Word Recognition Changes in Response to Difficulty has Independent Relevance
articles_hidden.authors: John Baltazar Muegge; Bob McMurray
articles_hidden.abstract: Listeners must often recognize words in challenging listening conditions like background noise. The cognitive mechanisms of spoken word recognition offer a potential locus for adaptation to such contexts. Indeed, research has found that the millisecond-by-millisecond dynamics of word recognition in challenging conditions differ lawfully along a small number of dimensions. However, comparatively little is known about the factors that impact the nature of an individual listener’s response to challenge. Here we ask if this response is stable across time and challenge type, if it is constrained by the idiosyncrasies of how listeners recognize words in quiet, and if these patterns of processing predict performance in real-world outcome measures. We tested listeners in a Visual World Paradigm with two different types of challenging listening across two days. We then leveraged a principal component analysis to extract underlying dimensions of variance across these conditions. Using this approach, we found that the dynamics of word recognition in challenge are predicted by their dynamics in typical speech, that these dynamics are stable across days and different types of challenge, and that the magnitude with which listeners change recognition predicts their performance in tests of speech-in-noise comprehension.

articles_hidden.title: Shared Dimensions, Divergent Patterns: Multidimensional Well-Being Among Cultural Majority and Minoritized Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Jozefien De Leersnyder
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents adapt constantly to their social environments, which can support certain functions while limiting others. In intercultural contexts, adolescents share institutions but hold different social positions and cultural references. Consequently, similar overall well-being scores can mask entirely different combinations of health, relationships, and material conditions—a limitation of single total scores. Well-being and acculturation research approach this problem differently. Well-being research provides broad theories but typically focuses on global indicators within Western majority samples, while acculturation research studies adaptation in intercultural contexts but primarily examines minorities and separates psychological adjustment from sociocultural competence. Researchers currently lack a common multidimensional framework to capture well-being variations among adolescents sharing an intercultural environment. We addressed this gap in 1,385 Belgian-majority and Turkish–Moroccan minoritized adolescents using exploratory and multigroup factor analyses, which supported a broadly comparable five-domain structure. This demonstrates that a common framework can apply across groups while accommodating meaningful differences in how well-being is experienced and organized. Item-level differences formed a mixed profile rather than a consistent advantage for either group. Cross-sectional Gaussian graphical models revealed differences in overall edge-weight structure and global strength, with greater aggregate connectivity in the Turkish–Moroccan network, though no individual edge difference survived correction. Across both groups, the strongest associations clustered within domains alongside cross-domain links. These findings suggest that adolescent well-being is better understood as a multidimensional system than as a single score: shared dimensions can coexist with different profiles and relational organization. Longitudinal research is needed to determine whether these patterns reflect contextual conditions, cultural orientations, or their interplay.

articles_hidden.title: Why We Cringe: Understanding the Function of Cringe in Social Cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Deutchman; Shaon Lahiri
articles_hidden.abstract: Cringe is an increasingly common term in social discourse and popular media, often used to describe situations perceived as awkward or uncomfortable, yet we understand little about its underlying psychology and function in social life. Across five studies (N = 1415; three preregistered), we examined cringe as both a stable individual difference and a situational response, testing whether it is distinct from vicarious embarrassment at the trait and situational levels. We propose that cringe is a variety of vicarious embarrassment elicited by intentional, reputationally damaging norm violations and grounded in observers’ inferences about the transgressor’s intent and associated with negative evaluations and social sanctioning. We first developed and validated the 20-item Cringe Scale, which predicted cringe perceptions, behavioral intentions, and incentivized donations. Trait cringe overlapped substantially with trait vicarious embarrassment, although the Cringe Scale’s inauthenticity component uniquely predicted cringe perceptions. At the situational level, however, the two diverged. Intent increased cringe more than vicarious embarrassment, and cringe was heightened for public versus private transgressions. Compared with vicarious embarrassment, cringe was associated with greater moral wrongness and punishment judgments and reduced empathy and prosocial motivation toward the transgressor. Perceived intent mediated the differences in moral wrongness and norm violation judgments. Together, our results suggest that cringe and vicarious embarrassment share a common dispositional basis but differ in their situational elicitors and social-cognitive consequences. These findings inform our understanding of an increasingly important self-conscious emotion and illuminate its role in social norm cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Dreading Tomorrow, Dreading Today:  Additive Effects of Evening Stress Anticipation and Sleep Quality on Morning Stress Anticipation
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Jori Lücke; Andreas B. Neubauer
articles_hidden.abstract: When people are expecting a stressful upcoming day, they tend to sleep poorly; sleeping poorly in turn has been linked to expecting a more stressful upcoming day. These mutual associations have led researchers to assume a mediating effect of evening stress anticipation on morning stress anticipation via nightly sleep. One important gap in these considerations is that people are likely able to predict how stressful the next day will be, as indicated by substantial associations of evening stress anticipation and next-day well-being irrespective of sleep. In the present study, we thus aim to disentangle time-ordered associations among evening stress anticipation, sleep, and morning stress anticipation in a 2-week ambulatory assessment study. A sample of 126 young adults (Mage = 21.5 years, SD = 2.7, 84.1% women) rated their stress anticipation for the upcoming day every evening and the next morning.
