Additionally, they reported their sleep quality and duration each morning and wore a smartwatch to track their sleep. Results from two-level structural equation models showed that evening stress anticipation predicted lower self-reported sleep quality, which predicted morning stress anticipation. The findings did not support a mediating process but rather an additive effect of sleep quality on morning stress anticipation beyond stability of evening stress anticipation. There were no significant association with smartwatch measured sleep. In conclusion, stress anticipation was rather stable overnight, but an additional effect of sleep quality suggests morning stress anticipation appraisals may be affected by reduced available resources following poor sleep.

articles_hidden.title: Poor Sleep, More Stress? Bidirectional Associations Between Sleep and Stress in Younger and Older Adults’ Daily Lives
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Jori Lücke; Malin Freidle; Wessel M.A. van Leeuwen; Göran Kecklund; Torbjörn Åkerstedt; Johanna Schwarz
articles_hidden.abstract: Insufficient sleep has been linked with increased daytime stress and vice versa. However, previous research had poor temporal resolution regarding daytime and evening stress, leaving open whether stress across the day is differentially associated with sleep. Additionally, age differences in associations between sleep and daily stress have rarely been considered. To analyze bidirectional associations between sleep and stress across the day, we used data from 161 younger (Mage = 23.8, SD = 3.0, 49.1% male) and 170 older adults (Mage = 63.6, SD = 5.69, 41.2% male) who completed a 21-day ambulatory assessment study. Participants wore an actigraph, reported on their sleep quality each morning, and rated their current stress levels up to eight times daily. Results from dynamic structural equation models showed that lower than usual sleep quality predicted higher stress across the first half of the day whereas shorter than usual sleep duration only predicted higher stress early in the morning and around midday. Higher than usual stress in the late evening predicted worse sleep quality and stress in the early afternoon and early evening partly predicted shorter sleep duration the following night. Younger and older adults showed similar associations between sleep and stress, suggesting that these associations generalize across adulthood. However, stress levels in this study were generally low-to-moderate and future research may consider whether stress shows a strong effect on sleep once it crosses a certain threshold. In summary, effects of sleep on subsequent stress were more consistent than those of stress on subsequent sleep.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Directed Generative AI Use and Academic Development Among Secondary School Students: A Large-Scale, One-Year Longitudinal Study
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Hübner; René F. Kizilcec; Lisa Bäulke; Ronny Scherer; Wolfgang Wagner; Benjamin Nagengast; Ulrich Trautwein; Jennifer Meyer
articles_hidden.abstract: Many students use generative AI (GenAI) tools for schoolwork on their own, without pedagogical guidance. Yet it remains unclear whether such use supports or undermines their academic development, or which students turn to it. We examined both questions using TOSCAneo data from 4,062 students in 136 secondary schools in Germany. Data were collected at the beginning and end of the 2023/2024 school year and included standardized achievement tests and measures of academic self-concept, value beliefs, and effort across six subjects. Students’ reported use of GenAI tools for academic activities formed two related factors: task-completion use and learning-oriented use. GenAI use increased over the school year for both task-completion use (d = 0.35) and learning-oriented use (d = 0.33), with only 5% of students never using GenAI. In cross-lagged panel models, lower prior achievement predicted more subsequent GenAI use in all six subjects for task-completion use and in five of six for learning-oriented use. Neither form of use predicted subsequent achievement. A use profile characterized by more task-completion and less learning-oriented use predicted lower subsequent effort in four of six subjects. No comparable pattern emerged for self-concept or value beliefs, and prior self-concept, value beliefs, and effort did not consistently predict later GenAI use. Overall, rather than predicting later achievement, self-directed GenAI use was related to which students turn to these tools and how much effort they invest. Guidance may therefore be particularly important for lower-achieving students, who use GenAI more than their higher-achieving peers.

articles_hidden.title: Does Early Childhood Education and Care for Infants and Toddlers Cause Behavior Problems Up to Age 8?
articles_hidden.authors: Henrik Daae Zachrisson; Eric Dearing; Nicolai T. Borgen
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: The causal effect of attending Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) for infants and toddlers on child behavior problems is contested. Yet, most previous research is correlational. Findings from previous research are mixed, but with some evidence of harmful effects on children’s behavior. Some correlational studies also suggest that ECEC may be most harmful for children from socioeconomically advantaged families. Methods: We estimate the effect of age of entry into ECEC on externalizing behavior problems at ages 3, 5, and 8 years in a large sample (n=66,394) from The Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort study (MoBa). We use two quasi-experimental methods, Two-Way Fixed-Effects models and Instrumental Variable models, that exploit variations in how early families enrolled their children in ECEC due to a national scale-up of publicly funded centers. Results: In this high-powered, rigorous approach to testing the causal impact of age of entry into ECEC, we find no evidence that entry around age 1 relative to later affects behavior problems either during preschool years (at ages 3 or 5) or after school entry (at age 8 years). We also find no evidence that these effects vary by parental education or family income. Conclusion: We find no evidence suggesting that early entry into ECEC has harmful consequences for children’s behavior regulation, during the preschool years or after school entry. We argue that our null results may be due to ECEC pedagogy in Norway that emphasizes young children’s well-being and playful learning experiences.

articles_hidden.title: Developing and Validating a Measurement Scale to Assess Knowledge of Memory and Learning Processes Among Italian Teachers
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Carabba; Ottavia M. Epifania; Demis Basso
articles_hidden.abstract:
Knowledge of memory and learning processes may inform teachers’ educational decisions. However, to our knowledge, no psychometrically validated instrument specifically assesses teachers’ procedural knowledge of these processes through realistic classroom scenarios.
This Stage 1 Registered Report aims to develop and validate a scenario-based measure of Italian teachers’ procedural knowledge of memory and learning processes.
Approximately 600 Italian teachers, from preschool to upper-secondary education, will be recruited through proportional stratified quota sampling based on sex, geographical area, and school level.
Following two pilot studies and iterative revisions, 30 original items were retained and paired with conceptually matched items to create two intended parallel forms. All participants will complete the 60 multiple-choice items online. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses will be conducted separately for each form in independent subsamples. Measurement invariance across forms will be examined if corresponding factor structures are supported. Internal consistency will be estimated using Cronbach’s alpha. Mixed-effects logistic regression will examine associations between item-level accuracy and teaching experience, educational attainment, and, among teachers with tertiary qualifications, academic field.
We expect interpretable, replicable factor structures and adequate internal consistency, with measurement invariance providing additional evidence of comparability across forms. Higher accuracy is tentatively expected with higher educational attainment, psycho-pedagogical qualifications, and fewer years of teaching experience.
The study will provide initial evidence on the psychometric properties of the proposed measure. If the findings support its validity and reliability, the instrument could subsequently be used to identify teachers’ knowledge gaps and inform teacher education initiatives.

articles_hidden.title: Student agency in higher education course contexts: A multidimensional and multilevel analysis of agency and its associations with teaching practices
articles_hidden.authors: Päivikki Jääskelä; Jingwen Jiang; Asko Tolvanen; Maarit Arvaja; Elina Vaara; Anna-Maija Poikkeus
articles_hidden.abstract: Comprehensive, empirically grounded, and multidimensional conceptualizations of student agency in higher education remain limited, constraining the accumulation of knowledge about how agency varies across contexts and relates to teaching. This study examines student agency within university courses. The study conceptualizes student agency as a dynamic capacity for purposeful learning and transformation, enabled by students’ perceived resources for agency, manifested in their agentic will, and realized through agentic action that advances individual learning, contributes to knowledge co-construction, and shapes the conditions for them. Using a validated questionnaire, we examined students’ perceptions of agency across 15 subdimensions representing these three components—resources for agency, agentic will and agentic action. The sample comprised 1,140 students from 47 courses at a Finnish university. We used multilevel modeling to analyze individual- and course-level variation in agency, interrelations among the subdimensions, and their associations with student-rated teaching practices. Mean levels of agency were generally moderate to high, but substantial variation emerged within and across courses. Some subdimensions, particularly opportunities for interaction as a resource, showed high between-course variation, indicating that course design shapes opportunities to practice agency. The three components and their subdimensions were moderately to strongly interrelated, supporting their conceptualization as analytically distinct yet mutually constitutive aspects of agency. Teaching practices, especially transparent course design, learning activities requiring higher-order thinking, and supervisory teacher roles, were positively associated with multiple subdimensions of agency. The study provides a multidimensional operationalization of student agency and advances understanding of how teaching practices can foster student agency in higher education.

articles_hidden.title: Why do we touch ourselves? A Hypothesis on How We Maintain the Bodily Self
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Boehme
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do we keep touching ourselves? Here, I propose the hypothesis that recurrent self-generated sensations may contribute to maintaining embodied self-experience by providing reliable evidence about the body as a source of action and sensation. Self-touch generates predictable sensory consequences of one's own actions, thereby potentially reinforcing bodily agency, ownership, self-location, and self-other-distinction. Within this account, sensory attenuation follows from successful prediction. Social touch extends this process beyond the individual, as sensory and affective signals are regulated between interacting bodies, highlighting the relational character of self-other-differentiation. The framework predicts that destabilizing bodily self-experience should increase self-evidence-generating behaviors, that reliable self-generated feedback should accelerate recovery, and that disrupting action-sensory contingency should abolish this benefit. Autism and schizophrenia illustrate how altered sensory and social conditions may interact with such self-maintenance processes.

articles_hidden.title: Group Membership Changes How Others’ Affect Informs Observers’ Valuation of Unseen Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Damon Dashti; Marius C. Vollberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Others’ affective reactions can be the only available information about how good an outcome might be, yet little is known about how people use them to inform their own valuation. Across three preregistered experiments, we tested how observers use others’ reactions to value unseen lottery outcomes, and whether social group membership changes this affect-based value inference. Participants observed facial reactions of “demonstrators” to hidden lottery outcomes, reported how good they believed the demonstrator felt about the outcome (inferred affect), and stated their incentive-compatible willingness to pay (WTP) for these lotteries. In Experiment 1 (N = 416), happy relative to neutral expressions increased both inferred affect and WTP, and inferred affect accounted for most of the valuation difference. Experiment 2 (N = 1,127; informed by piloting, N = 419) introduced group membership via political agreement. In-group demonstrators were inferred to feel slightly better, and happy expressions increased WTP more when they came from in-group than from out-group demonstrators. Experiment 3 (N = 1,461) replicated these findings and added angry expressions, which reduced WTP without significant group differences. Across Experiments 2 and 3, group differences in reported inferred affect partially accounted for the group differences in valuation. Our findings extend affect’s role as a social signal to economic valuation and show that social group membership changes how others’ reactions inform observers’ valuation of unseen outcomes. Affect may thus be one route by which preferences spread differently within identity-aligned groups.

articles_hidden.title: School-based Mental Health and Wellbeing in Adolescents: An Umbrella Review
articles_hidden.authors: René Droomer; Colin M Gorman; Emily McGlinchey
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract

Background
Adolescent mental disorders affect approximately 15% of young people worldwide with a stark rise in mental health difficulties in secondary school age children over the past decade. Need for psychological support exceeds available provision and is exacerbated by staffing shortages. Schools are key settings for mental health and wellbeing (MHWB) support. This umbrella review synthesises evidence on school-based MHWB interventions in secondary schools, aiming to map and evaluate outcomes and intervention approaches on a tiered framework. 

Methods
Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of reviews on school-based MHWB interventions was conducted. Data were extracted on intervention type, delivery mode, and outcomes. Reviews including broader age ranges (4-25 years) were considered, with a specific focus on adolescents.

Results
After screening 478 studies, 33 reviews published between 2014 and 2024 were included, covering programmes for adolescents aged 12-18 years. Social and emotional learning (SEL) programmes were most effective when implemented as whole-school approaches. Targeted interventions produced the largest gains for high-risk students, while universal programmes were more common in younger age groups. Preventive interventions delivered by specialists showed stronger effects, whereas universal programmes were more effective when delivered by school staff. Findings support a stepped-care model aligning MHWB support to student need. However, despite policy recommendations, implementation remains inconsistent.

Conclusions
Effective MHWB provision in schools requires culturally responsive, developmentally appropriate, and scalable approaches. A tiered framework matching support to student need is recommended. Future research should explore digital delivery, scalability, and sustainability of school-based MHWB initiatives.

Keywords: Adolescent mental health; School-based interventions; Social and emotional learning; Stepped care; Secondary schools; Preventive interventions; Digital mental health.

articles_hidden.title: Testing the Relationship between Phenomenological Control related to Illusion Sensitivity
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Makowski; Ana Neves
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual illusions highlight how easily our conscious experience can be altered with respect to perceptual reality. Despite sharing in-principle mechanisms with phenomenological control, i.e., the ability to alter our perceptual experience to match task demands or expectations, research tying the two remains scarce. This study aimed to replicate and extend Lush et al. (2022) by testing for a relationship between phenomenological control and illusion sensitivity across multiple illusion types, assessing the role of higher-level (top-down) processes. It also examined associations between visual illusion sensitivity and psychoticism to assess the potential contribution of lower-level effects (e.g., weak priors). Five hundred participants were recruited in an online study using an illusion-based perceptual decision paradigm (Illusion Game; Makowski et al., 2023) measuring sensitivity to three visual illusions (Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer, Vertical-Horizontal), alongside the Phenomenological Control Scale and personality measures. In the registered analysis (N = 295), Bayesian correlations provided evidence against a relationship between phenomenological control and error rates for the Müller-Lyer and Ebbinghaus illusions, but were inconclusive for the Vertical-Horizontal illusion. The data also favoured the absence of the hypothesised association between error rates and psychoticism. These conclusions were unchanged in an unregistered sensitivity analysis addressing data quality issues. These findings are consistent with the cognitive impenetrability of these two illusions under the present task conditions, and suggest that susceptibility to them is not related to trait-level control over subjective experience. However, low consistency across illusion measures highlights important methodological limitations in capturing individual differences related to illusion sensitivity.

articles_hidden.title: A Call to Action: Open and Inclusive Assessment Measures in Developmental Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Marta Topor; Lucija Batinovic; Emily Kate Farran; Lucy A. Henry; Magnus Ivarsson; Jo Van Herwegen; David Messer; Karin Nilsson; Lisa Palmqvist; Caroline Richards
articles_hidden.abstract:
Cognitive and behavioural development research often relies on validated and standardised assessments, which can indicate whether performance falls within typical or atypical boundaries for a given chronological age. However, researchers planning large collaborative projects and/or collecting data from hard-to-reach populations may face problems when attempting to use some of the most widely adopted measures. We outline the major consequences of restricting access and preventing modifications of measures for research in the fields of developmental psychology and education. The problems are illustrated using a case example of a big team science project on intellectual disability. Finally, a plan for collective action to establish public domain assessment tools is presented with specific recommendations for research funders and researchers. In the interest of scientific progression and international collaboration, we conclude that there should be opportunities for free access to research measures and their unrestricted adaptation and modification.

articles_hidden.title: Conceptualizing Duration: A Corpus-Based Study of Distance and Quantity Metaphors of Time in Japanese
articles_hidden.authors: Daisuke Abe; Junya Fukuta
articles_hidden.abstract: Languages differ in how they describe temporal duration, often drawing on metaphors of spatial distance (e.g., long/short) or quantity (e.g., much/little). Previous cross-linguistic comparisons have relied on search frequencies for a limited set of expressions, potentially overlooking the lexical diversity and contextual variation of temporal metaphors. This study investigates the distribution of distance- and quantity-based duration metaphors in Japanese using the Balanced Corpus of Contemporary Written Japanese (BCCWJ). Through dependency parsing, we systematically extracted adjectives modifying jikan ('time') and manually examined their contexts to identify and classify metaphorical expressions of duration. Of the 1,035 expressions identified, 839 (81.1%) were distance-based, whereas 196 (18.9%) were quantity-based. Distance metaphors were dominated by nagai ('long') and mijikai ('short'), while quantity metaphors involved a wider variety of less frequent adjectives. These findings demonstrate a clear preference for distance-based expressions in Japanese, resembling patterns previously reported for English. More importantly, our approach reveals patterns of metaphorical usage that cannot be adequately captured by simple searches for predetermined expressions. By combining dependency parsing with contextual analysis, this study provides a more comprehensive and systematic method for investigating temporal metaphors, offering a basis for more precise cross-linguistic comparisons.

articles_hidden.title: Agreement with Collective Nouns in L2 English: Effects of Syntax, Dialect, and Frequency
articles_hidden.authors: Hunter Brakovec; Tom Rankin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Within the second language (L2) acquisition field, there is a large divide between generative/formal approaches and variationist approaches. In this study, we attempt to unite these approaches by implementing a sociosyntactic approach which adopts aspects of both formal and variationist research. Specifically, we examine the acquisition of verbal agreement with collective nouns by French and German learners of L2 English. On the formal side, we investigate how universal restrictions on Agree, i.e., c-command, constrain the availability of plural agreement. On the variationist side, we explore how differences in exposure to American vs. British English affect the acceptance of plural agreement. We find that plural agreement is largely rejected by both L2 groups. Still, the German learners display sensitivity to the universal constraints on Agree. While the French learners do not, their behavior also did not violate these constraints. Furthermore, while we find an effect of dialect exposure, it was the opposite of what 
was predicted: those learners exposed to more American English rated plural agreement higher. We ultimately argue that future research should continue to adopt the sociosyntactic approach to gain a fuller understanding of the L2 acquisition process.

articles_hidden.title: Can Digital Mental Health Support Meet the Needs of Autistic People? A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Dawn Adams; Chris Paradisis; Kiera Louise Adams
articles_hidden.abstract:
Autistic people experience high rates of mental health conditions and barriers to accessing supports. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may be one way to improve access, but their applicability is unclear. We reviewed DMHIs that focus on mental health outcomes in autistic people, examining their scope, adaptation, community involvement and evidence of effectiveness.
Five databases were searched in 08/2024 and 04/2026. Eligible studies evaluated a DMHI and reported pre-post mental health outcomes in autistic people. Findings were synthesised narratively using SWiM guidelines. Thirty-three studies reported on 1,258 autistic participants across fifteen studies were randomised controlled trials and 17 uncontrolled designs. Although anxiety was the primary focus of DMHIs, effects of DMHIs on depression, specific phobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder and trauma were also explored. Comparative findings for anxiety were mixed, and the predominantly small and uncontrolled evidence base could not establish efficacy. Most interventions were CBT-based, community involvement in study or DMHI design was very limited. DMHIs could be a promising option to support the mental health of autistic people, but research is in preliminary stages. Future studies should focus on co-producing DMHIs and embedding these into adequately powered controlled studies that are inclusive for a broader range of participants.

articles_hidden.title: French Translation and Validation of the Job Search Self-Efficacy Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte Rauscher; Charly Marie
articles_hidden.abstract: Job Search Self-Efficacy (JSSE), the belief that one can perform job search behavior and obtain employment, is a central determinant of the job search process. However, there is no validated French measure of JSSE. We translated and validated the JSSE scale (Saks et al., 2015) in French using a forward-backward translation procedure and addressed four limitations of previous studies. First, a large sample of 2,055 unemployed people answered the survey rather than small or student samples. Second, we used administrative records to measure objective job search behavior and access to employment instead of self-reports. Third, we used a longitudinal design at respectively 90- and 150-days instead of a cross-sectional design. Finally, we randomly withheld the survey from half of the sample to rule out a measurement effect. A confirmatory factor analysis supported the expected two-factor structure, which showed strict invariance across age, gender, education, and length of registration as well as scalar invariance after one month. Both subscales were reliable and stable over one month and correlated with self-esteem, autonomous motivation, and amotivation to (re)work in the expected direction and strength. When both subscales were entered jointly, JSSE behavior predicted the number of sent applications within 90 days, while JSSE outcome predicted access to temporary agency work within 150 days. This pattern is consistent with self-efficacy operating as a proximal correlate of job search behavior but a distal correlate of employment. The French JSSE is a reliable and structurally sound measure.

articles_hidden.title: Accelerometer-Derived Rest–Activity Rhythms and Sleep Disturbance in Older Adults: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study
articles_hidden.authors: Kyungmi Lee; Jennifer B. Levin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: To examine associations between accelerometer-derived rest–activity indicators and sleep disturbance among older adults.
Methods: This analysis included 1,373 person-wave observations from 569 National Health and Aging Trends Study participants. Multilevel models separated within-person and between-person components of the least active five-hour period (L5), coefficient of variation, and behavioral fragmentation. Relative amplitude (RA) was included at the between-person level in the primary model and examined separately in sensitivity analyses.
Results: In primary analyses, no rest–activity indicator was associated with sleep disturbance, including when sleep medication use was excluded; within-person estimates were small (95% CI bounds within ±0.031). Weak between-person associations for L5 and RA emerged only in exploratory, model-dependent analyses. Pain, depressive symptoms, chronic disease burden, and educational attainment were associated with sleep disturbance.
Conclusion: Rest–activity indicators showed no clear association with self-reported sleep disturbance, and small between-person estimates were model-dependent. Health-related and socioeconomic factors warrant attention in population-based sleep research.

articles_hidden.title: When Does Reputation Help the Future? Audience Presence and Identity Disclosure in Intergenerational Resource Dilemmas
articles_hidden.authors: Mingyuan Sheng; Ye Niu; Xiaoli Ling
articles_hidden.abstract: Many environmental problems, from climate change to resource depletion, are intergenerational dilemmas: the present generation bears conservation costs, whereas the benefits go to future generations, who can neither observe nor reciprocate. Reputation reliably sustains cooperation among contemporaries, but whether it works across generations remains unclear. In two experiments using an intergenerational goods game, we examined how the audience of disclosure and the type of information disclosed affect contributions to a resource passed from one generation to the next, and whether social value orientation (SVO) moderates these effects. In Experiment 1, disclosing to the next generation what participants had contributed increased the rate of sustained generations but did not reliably increase individual contributions or narrow the gap between prosocial and proself individuals. In Experiment 2, disclosing the same information to present peers increased both individual contributions and the rate of sustained generations. Adding names and faces was tentatively associated with a further increase in contributions, although this condition was recruited in a separate wave. These gains came mainly from proself individuals, whose contributions no longer differed from those of prosocial individuals when names and faces were disclosed. The findings suggest that disclosure promotes intergenerational cooperation chiefly when it reaches an audience present at the time of decision, and that identifiability matters most for those least motivated to cooperate. Making conservation visible to future generations may not be enough; it may also need to be visible to someone now, suggesting a potentially low-cost approach to promoting environmental cooperation.

articles_hidden.title: The effect of bereavement and prolonged grief on anger and physical aggression in parentally bereaved adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Parental bereavement is associated with adverse mental health and behavioral outcomes, yet its effects on anger and physical aggression remain unclear. This study examined the cross-sectional and longitudinal associations of parental bereavement and prolonged grief with anger and physical aggression.
Methods: Participants included 380 adolescents and young adults (mean age = 13.3 years, 49.2% female), comprising 206 parentally bereaved and 174 nonbereaved controls. Participants and their caregivers completed clinical assessments at baseline (approximately 9 months after parental death) and four follow-ups at approximately 21, 33, 62, and 84 months after death. 
Results: After adjustment for covariates, bereavement was not significantly associated with anger at baseline (β = 0.151, SE = 0.099, p = 0.127), and changes in anger over time did not differ between bereaved and nonbereaved participants (β = 0.001, SE = 0.001, p = 0.348). Bereavement was not significantly associated with physical aggression. Among bereaved participants, clinical prolonged grief was associated with higher anger at baseline (β = 0.516, SE = 0.163, p = 0.002) and greater increases in anger over time (β = 0.009, SE = 0.004, p = 0.038), but not with physical aggression. Physical aggression increased more steeply following sudden natural parental death than parental suicide (β = −0.187, SE = 0.081, p = 0.022).
Conclusions: Clinical prolonged grief, rather than bereavement alone, was associated with greater anger, whereas parental cause of death was associated with changes in physical aggression. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing emotional and behavioral expressions of aggression and assessing prolonged grief and family functioning following parental death.
